title: Volcanoes and earthquakes: why the ground shakes and burns where it does

summary.text: The ground under your feet feels still, yet it is travelling north-east by about 5 centimetres every year. The Earth's hard outer shell is broken into huge plates that move, stick and suddenly slip. In this lesson you pull a weighted box with a rubber band to find out if anyone can tell when it will jump. You follow India's own journey, from the lava floods of the Deccan to the rise of the Himalaya, the Bhuj earthquake, the 2004 tsunami and the volcano on Barren Island. You also find out what scientists can tell us before the ground shakes, and what nobody can.
summary.art: A cut-away side view of India riding on a thick slab of rock that pushes under the Himalaya, with a small smoking island volcano far out in the sea on the right and a child standing on the surface holding a rubber band.

intro.hook: On the top of Mount Everest, the rock is full of sea shells. The highest place on Earth was once the bottom of a sea. How did a sea floor get nearly 9 kilometres up into the sky?
intro.text: Nobody carried it there. The ground did it, moving more slowly than your fingernails grow. The same slow movement shook Bhuj in 2001, sent the sea over the coast of Tamil Nadu in 2004, and feeds a volcano that still smokes in the Andaman Sea. In this lesson you first draw the Earth to its true scale and see how thin the ground really is. Then you pull a heavy box with a rubber band and try to say when it will jump. That small test holds the biggest honest answer about earthquakes.
intro.art: A close view of a grey mountain rock with clear spiral and fan-shaped sea shell fossils in it, snow peaks behind, and a child's hand pointing at one shell.

outcomes: I can describe the layers inside the Earth, and say how we know about them without ever having seen them.
I can explain what a plate is, how fast plates move, and what happens at the three kinds of plate edge.
I can explain an earthquake as stick, stretch and slip, and use the words focus, epicentre, seismic wave and magnitude.
I can explain how a volcano forms, and why some pour out lava gently while others explode.
I can use a map to show why most earthquakes and volcanoes lie in lines, and I can name places that do not fit the lines.
I can tell India's own story: the journey of the Indian plate, the Deccan Traps, the Himalaya, Bhuj in 2001, the tsunami of 2004 and Barren Island.
I can say what scientists can and cannot tell us before an earthquake, and what to do when the ground shakes or the sea pulls back.

terms.meaning: The thin, hard, outer layer of rock that we live on. It is 5 to 10 kilometres thick under the oceans and 30 to 70 kilometres thick under the land.
terms.example: The granite under Bengaluru is part of the crust.
terms.art: A slice of the Earth with the thinnest outer line coloured brown and a tiny house standing on it.

terms.meaning: The thick layer of hot rock under the crust. It is solid, but over millions of years it creeps like very stiff dough.
terms.example: The mantle goes down about 2,900 kilometres, which is most of the way to the core.
terms.art: A slice of the Earth with the wide middle layer coloured orange, with slow curved arrows inside it.

terms.meaning: The centre of the Earth, made mostly of iron and nickel. The outer core is liquid. The inner core is solid.
terms.example: The inner core is hotter than 5,000 degrees Celsius, about as hot as the surface of the Sun.
terms.art: A slice of the Earth with a yellow liquid ring and a white solid ball at the centre.

terms.meaning: A huge slab made of the crust and the stiff top of the mantle. The Earth's outer shell is broken into about seven very large plates and many smaller ones.
terms.example: India, Sri Lanka and part of the Indian Ocean floor ride on the Indian plate.
terms.art: A globe drawn like a cracked egg shell, with the piece carrying India coloured green.

terms.meaning: The place where two plates meet. Scientists also call it a plate boundary. Plates move apart, push together or slide past each other there.
terms.example: The Himalaya stand along the edge where the Indian plate meets the plate that carries most of Asia.
terms.art: Two slabs of rock meeting, with three small sketches: arrows apart, arrows together, arrows sliding past.

terms.meaning: A crack in rock where the two sides have moved past each other.
terms.example: The Bhuj earthquake of 2001 came from a fault hidden deep under Kutch.
terms.art: A block of layered rock with a slanting crack, where the layers on one side sit higher than on the other.

terms.meaning: The shaking of the ground when stuck rock suddenly slips along a fault.
terms.example: Instruments pick up about half a million earthquakes every year. People feel only about one in five of them.
terms.art: A street with a wavy line running through the ground under the buildings.

terms.meaning: The place under the ground where the rock first slips in an earthquake.
terms.example: The focus of the Bhuj earthquake was about 16 kilometres below the ground.
terms.art: A side view of the ground with a star deep on a fault and rings spreading out from it.

terms.meaning: The place on the surface straight above the focus.
terms.example: The epicentre of the 2004 earthquake was in the sea, west of the island of Sumatra.
terms.art: The same side view with a dot on the surface straight above the star and a dotted line joining them.

terms.meaning: A wave of shaking that travels through the Earth from an earthquake. P waves push and stretch the rock and arrive first. S waves shake it from side to side and arrive second.
terms.example: P waves from an earthquake in Japan reach India in about ten minutes.
terms.art: A spring toy being pushed along its length beside a rope being flicked side to side.

terms.meaning: An instrument that draws the shaking of the ground as a wiggly line.
terms.example: A seismograph in Hyderabad can record an earthquake in Indonesia that nobody in Hyderabad feels.
terms.art: A drum of paper with a pen drawing a line that turns from flat to tall zigzags.

terms.meaning: A number for the size of an earthquake at its source. Each step up of one whole number means ten times more ground movement.
terms.example: Bhuj in 2001 was magnitude 7.7. The earthquake of 2004 was magnitude 9.1.
terms.art: A row of zigzag lines, each ten times taller than the one before, marked 5, 6 and 7.

terms.meaning: Melted rock under the ground, with gases mixed into it.
terms.example: Magma collects in a chamber a few kilometres under Barren Island.
terms.art: A side view of a volcano with a glowing pool deep below it and a pipe rising from the pool.

terms.meaning: Magma that has come out onto the surface.
terms.example: The dark rock of the Deccan was once lava that flowed across the land.
terms.art: A glowing stream running down a dark slope and turning into black rock at its edges.

terms.meaning: An opening in the crust where magma, ash and gases come out, and the hill that builds up around it.
terms.example: Barren Island, 138 kilometres from Port Blair, is India's active volcano.
terms.art: A cone-shaped island in the sea with a crater at the top and a plume of ash.

terms.meaning: A set of very long sea waves made when the sea floor suddenly moves, most often in an undersea earthquake. The word is Japanese for harbour wave.
terms.example: The tsunami of 26 December 2004 reached the coast of Tamil Nadu about two and a half hours after the earthquake.
terms.art: A side view of the sea where a step in the sea floor lifts the whole depth of water into a long low wave that grows tall at the shore.

terms.meaning: A place where volcanoes form far from any plate edge, above rock that is unusually hot.
terms.example: Hawaii sits on a hot spot in the middle of the Pacific plate.
terms.art: A plate sliding over a fixed glowing patch, leaving a line of islands of which only the newest smokes.

explanations.concept: Inside the Earth: crust, mantle and core
explanations.definition: The Earth has layers. From the outside in they are the crust, the mantle, the liquid outer core and the solid inner core.
explanations.description: It is about 6,370 kilometres from your feet to the centre of the Earth. The crust you stand on is the thinnest layer. If the Earth were a mango, the crust would be thinner than the skin. Under it lies the mantle, about 2,900 kilometres of hot rock. The mantle is solid. It is not a sea of lava. But it is so hot, and squeezed so hard, that over millions of years it creeps by a few centimetres a year. Below the mantle is the outer core, an ocean of liquid iron and nickel. At the centre is the inner core, a ball of solid metal that is hotter than 5,000 degrees Celsius. The heat comes from two places. Some is left over from the time the Earth formed. Some is made all the time by atoms deep in the rock that break apart and give out heat.
examples: The deepest hole ever drilled is the Kola borehole in Russia. It reached 12 kilometres in 1989, and it never left the crust.
At Koyna in Maharashtra, Indian scientists have drilled 3 kilometres into the Deccan rock to study earthquakes.
The liquid iron moving in the outer core makes the Earth a giant magnet, which is why a compass needle points north.
explanations.art: A wedge cut from the Earth, drawn to scale, with the crust as a hair-thin line, the wide mantle, the liquid outer core and the solid inner core, each marked with its depth in kilometres.
explanations.context: This card says what the Earth is made of on the inside. You need it to understand where the heat and the push for volcanoes and earthquakes come from.

perspectives.who: Seismologists, from Richard Oldham in 1906 to Inge Lehmann in 1936
perspectives.explanation: Nobody has seen below the crust. The layers were found by reading earthquake waves that had passed through the Earth. Oldham saw that waves slow down and bend deep inside, so there must be a core. Lehmann, working in Denmark, saw faint waves in a zone where none should arrive. She showed that they had bounced off a solid inner core.

perspectives.who: Scientists who squeeze and heat rock in laboratories
perspectives.explanation: Solid and liquid are not two clean boxes. The same mantle rock rings like a bell when an earthquake wave passes in a second, so it is solid. Over a million years it flows. The answer depends on how long you watch.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study what the core is made of
perspectives.explanation: The core is lighter than pure iron and nickel would be. Something else is mixed in. It may be sulphur, oxygen, silicon or hydrogen. Nobody has a sample, so this is still argued.

explanations.concept: Plates: the broken shell that moves
explanations.definition: A plate is a huge slab of the crust and the stiff top of the mantle. The plates move a few centimetres every year, carrying the land and the sea floor with them.
explanations.description: The hard outer shell of the Earth is not one piece. It is broken into about seven very large plates and many smaller ones, a little like the shell of a boiled egg that has been cracked all over. The plates are 50 to 250 kilometres thick. They ride on mantle rock that is softer and creeps. Most plates move between 2 and 10 centimetres a year, which is about as fast as your fingernails grow. That sounds like nothing. But in a million years, 5 centimetres a year adds up to 50 kilometres. Satellites now measure this movement directly. A marker fixed to the rock in Bengaluru moves about 5 centimetres towards the north-east every year, along with all of India.
examples: The Indian plate carries India, Sri Lanka and a large part of the Indian Ocean floor.
The Pacific plate is the largest. It is almost all sea floor.
A child who is 9 years old has travelled about 45 centimetres with the Indian plate since she was born.
explanations.art: A world map with the plates outlined like pieces of a cracked shell, each with an arrow showing which way it moves, and the Indian plate coloured.
explanations.context: This card explains the one idea that ties volcanoes, earthquakes and mountains together: the ground is broken into plates, and the plates move.

perspectives.who: Alfred Wegener, a German weather scientist, in 1912
perspectives.explanation: He said the continents were once joined and had drifted apart. He pointed to coastlines that fit, and to the same fossils on lands now far apart. Most geologists of his time rejected the idea, because he could not say what force could move a continent.

perspectives.who: Scientists who say sinking plates do the pulling, for example Donald Forsyth and Seiya Uyeda in 1975
perspectives.explanation: Old sea floor is cold and heavy. Where it dives into the mantle, it sinks and drags the rest of its plate behind it. They found that plates with a long diving edge move fastest, so this pull seems to be the main force.

perspectives.who: Scientists who say the creeping mantle does the carrying
perspectives.explanation: Hot mantle rock rises, spreads sideways and sinks again, very slowly. In this view the plates are carried along on top. Most scientists now think both things happen, and they still argue about how much each one does.

explanations.concept: Three things plates do at their edges
explanations.definition: Where two plates meet, they move apart, push together or slide past each other. Each kind of edge makes its own kind of land, earthquake and volcano.
explanations.description: Where plates move apart, hot mantle rock rises into the gap, melts and cools into new sea floor. This happens along the mid-ocean ridges, which form the longest mountain chain on Earth, almost all of it under water. Where plates push together, one of two things happens. If one plate is heavy sea floor, it dives under the other and sinks into the mantle. Water carried down with it helps the rock above to melt, and a line of volcanoes grows. If both plates carry light continent rock, neither can dive. The rock between them crumples and piles up into mountains. Where plates slide past each other, no rock is made or lost. The edges catch and stick, then jerk forward, and the ground shakes.
examples: Moving apart: the Carlsberg Ridge under the Arabian Sea, where the Indian plate moves away from Africa.
Pushing together with one plate diving: under the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, where the Indian plate dives beneath the Burma plate.
Pushing together with no plate diving: the Himalaya, where India meets Asia.
Sliding past: the San Andreas fault in California.
explanations.art: Three small side views in a row: two plates moving apart with rock rising between, one plate diving under another with a volcano above, and two plates sliding past each other with a broken road across them.
explanations.context: This card sorts plate edges into three kinds. It helps you guess what you will find at any edge on the map.

perspectives.who: School books and most maps
perspectives.explanation: They draw each plate edge as one thin line and give it one of three names. This is a good first map, and it explains most volcanoes and earthquakes.

perspectives.who: Geologists who measure the ground with satellites, such as Richard Gordon and Seth Stein
perspectives.explanation: Many edges are not lines. They are belts hundreds of kilometres wide. The squeeze between India and Asia is spread from the Himalaya across Tibet and far into China. The Indian plate itself is slowly breaking under the Indian Ocean, and no single line marks the break.

explanations.concept: Why the ground shakes: stick, stretch and slip
explanations.definition: An earthquake happens when rock that was stuck along a fault suddenly slips. The energy stored in the bent rock is let go as waves of shaking.
explanations.description: Plates never stop moving, but their edges do not glide. Rock is rough, and friction holds the two sides of a fault together. So the plate keeps moving while its edge stays stuck. The rock near the fault bends, the way a ruler bends when you push its two ends. Rock can bend a little and store energy, just like a stretched rubber band. This can go on for a hundred years or more. Then the stuck patch gives way. The two sides jump past each other, by a few centimetres in a small earthquake and by 10 to 20 metres in a great one. The place where the slip starts is the focus. The slip can then run along the fault for hundreds of kilometres in a few minutes. The stored energy travels out as seismic waves, and that is the shaking people feel.
examples: In 2004 the fault off Sumatra slipped along about 1,300 kilometres. The slipping took nearly ten minutes.
After a big earthquake, the rock nearby settles with many smaller earthquakes called aftershocks.
A door that sticks and then flies open when you push harder is a small stick and slip.
explanations.art: Three drawings of a fence crossing a fault: straight, then bent into a curve as the two sides move, then broken and straight again with the two halves offset.
explanations.context: This card explains what an earthquake is. It is the idea you test with the box and the rubber band.

perspectives.who: Harry Fielding Reid, an American scientist, in 1910
perspectives.explanation: After the San Francisco earthquake of 1906, he compared old and new land surveys. The land on both sides of the fault had been bending slowly for decades, and it sprang back in the earthquake. He called this elastic rebound. It is still the main explanation.

perspectives.who: Varahamihira, an astronomer of Ujjain, in the Brihat Samhita, in the 500s CE
perspectives.explanation: His chapter on earthquakes sets side by side the explanations of earlier scholars. They include giant animals living in the water, the tired elephants who hold up the Earth, winds crashing into each other, and a cause that cannot be seen. He recorded them without choosing one.

perspectives.who: Peoples who live with earthquakes
perspectives.explanation: In Japan, stories tell of a giant catfish named Namazu who thrashes under the land. The Maori of New Zealand speak of Ruaumoko, the unborn child of the Earth mother, turning over. These stories kept the memory of past earthquakes alive for the people who came later.

explanations.concept: Seismic waves, and two ways to measure an earthquake
explanations.definition: Seismic waves carry the energy of an earthquake through the Earth. Magnitude measures the size of the earthquake at its source. Intensity measures how hard the ground shook at one place.
explanations.description: An earthquake sends out several kinds of waves. P waves push and stretch the rock along the way they travel, like a push sent along a spring toy. They are the fastest, at about 6 kilometres every second in the crust, and they pass through solids and liquids. S waves shake the rock from side to side. They travel at about 4 kilometres every second, and they do not pass through liquids. Surface waves are the slowest. They roll along the ground and do most of the damage. A seismograph draws all of them as a wiggly line. Seismologists use the line to work out the magnitude. Each step of one whole number means the ground moved ten times more, and about 32 times more energy was let go. Intensity is different. It describes what people felt and what broke at one place, so one earthquake has one magnitude but many intensities.
examples: The gap between the P wave and the S wave tells how far away the earthquake was, in the way the gap between lightning and thunder tells how far away a storm is.
A magnitude 7 earthquake moves the ground 100 times more than a magnitude 5.
The Bhuj earthquake shook the ground very hard near Bhachau and gently in Mumbai. It was the same earthquake, with the same magnitude.
explanations.art: A seismograph trace with three labelled parts: a small first wiggle marked P, a larger one marked S, and the tallest waves marked surface waves.
explanations.context: This card explains the waves an earthquake sends out and the numbers used to describe it. You need it to read earthquake news correctly.

perspectives.who: Seismologists such as Hiroo Kanamori and Thomas Hanks, in 1979
perspectives.explanation: They measure an earthquake by how large the slipped patch of fault was and how far it slipped. This is called moment magnitude. It replaced the scale Charles Richter made in 1935, which could not tell the largest earthquakes apart.

perspectives.who: Engineers and the people who lived through it
perspectives.explanation: For them the number that matters is how hard their own ground shook. A middle-sized earthquake under a city on soft soil can do more harm than a huge one far out at sea. The Latur earthquake of 1993 was only magnitude 6.2, and nearly 8,000 people died, because stone houses fell on sleeping families.

explanations.concept: Volcanoes: where melted rock reaches the top
explanations.definition: A volcano is an opening in the crust where magma, ash and gases come out, together with the hill of cooled lava and ash that builds up around the opening.
explanations.description: Most of the mantle is solid, so magma has to be made. Rock melts in a few kinds of places. It melts where hot rock rises and the squeeze on it drops. It melts where a diving plate carries water down, because wet rock melts more easily. Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it rises and collects in a chamber. Magma has gases dissolved in it, like the fizz in a closed bottle of soda. When magma is runny, the gas bubbles escape easily. Lava pours out and spreads far, building wide, low hills. When magma is thick and sticky, the bubbles are trapped. The push of the gas builds until the magma is blown apart into ash, and a steep cone grows. People sort volcanoes into active, dormant and extinct. An active volcano has erupted in recent times. A dormant one is quiet but may erupt again. An extinct one is not expected to erupt again.
examples: Runny lava: the volcanoes of Hawaii, and the lava floods of the Deccan.
Sticky magma: Krakatau in Indonesia, which blew itself apart in 1883.
Barren Island in the Andaman Sea is active. Narcondam, its neighbour, is dormant.
explanations.art: A cut-away volcano with a magma chamber, a pipe, a crater, layers of old lava and ash, and beside it two small sketches: a wide low hill and a steep cone.
explanations.context: This card explains what a volcano is and why volcanoes behave so differently. You test the runny and sticky idea with batter and a straw.

perspectives.who: Volcano scientists, for example at the Smithsonian's Global Volcanism Program
perspectives.explanation: They do not trust the words dormant and extinct. A volcano's life is far longer than written history. They count any volcano that has erupted in about the last 12,000 years as one that could erupt again. Barren Island was quiet for well over a century, and then it erupted in 1991.

perspectives.who: People who live on volcanoes
perspectives.explanation: In Hawaii, the volcano is Pele, a powerful being who destroys land and makes new land. Farmers on the slopes of Merapi in Java know the mountain as a danger and also as the giver of their rich soil. They see one being with two sides, not a disaster.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study the early Earth
perspectives.explanation: They see volcanoes as makers. Over billions of years, volcanoes brought up gases that helped to build the air, and rock that became the land. Where the Earth's first water came from is still argued.

explanations.concept: Why they happen where they do: lines on the map, and places that break the rule
explanations.description: Mark the world's earthquakes and volcanoes on a map, and they do not fall everywhere. They fall in narrow belts, and the belts are the plate edges. The edge of the Pacific Ocean has so many that it is called the Ring of Fire. About three out of four active volcanoes on land are there, and most of the world's earthquakes. But some do not fit. Hawaii sits in the middle of a plate. So do the old volcanoes of the Deccan. These are called hot spots, and scientists argue about what feeds them. Earthquakes also strike inside plates. Bhuj is about 400 kilometres from the nearest plate edge. Latur and Koyna are deep inside the Indian plate. India is being squeezed as it pushes into Asia, and old faults far inside the plate can slip under that squeeze. Such earthquakes are rarer, and they are harder to forecast.
examples: On the line: Japan, Indonesia, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Nepal, Chile.
Off the line: Hawaii, Bhuj in 2001, Latur in 1993, Koyna in 1967.
At Koyna the earthquakes began after a large dam was filled, so people can set off earthquakes too.
explanations.art: A world map with red triangles for volcanoes and blue dots for earthquakes falling into narrow belts along plate edges, with Hawaii, Bhuj and Latur circled as places off the belts.
explanations.context: This card answers the question in the title of the lesson. It also shows honestly where the plate idea is not enough.

perspectives.who: W. Jason Morgan, in 1971, and most geologists today
perspectives.explanation: A hot spot is fed by a plume, a narrow column of hot rock rising all the way from the bottom of the mantle. The plate slides over it, and a chain of volcanoes is left behind, each older than the last.

perspectives.who: Gillian Foulger and other scientists who doubt deep plumes
perspectives.explanation: Many hot spots do not show a clear column of hot rock below them. In this view the plate is being stretched and cracked from the side, and shallow rock melts and leaks up through the cracks.

perspectives.who: Seismologists who study earthquakes inside plates, such as Harsh Gupta in India
perspectives.explanation: Places like Kutch are old tears in the plate from the time India broke away from other lands. They are weak places. The steady squeeze from the north loads them slowly, perhaps over thousands of years, and then one slips.

explanations.concept: India's journey: from Gondwana to the Himalaya
explanations.definition: India was once part of a great southern land called Gondwana. It broke away, crossed an ocean, and pushed into Asia. The Himalaya are the rock crumpled up between the two.
explanations.description: About 180 million years ago, India was joined to Africa, Antarctica, Australia and Madagascar. The name Gondwana comes from the land of the Gond people of central India, where the first clues were found in the rocks. Gondwana cracked apart. About 88 million years ago India left Madagascar behind and moved north, for a time at more than 15 centimetres a year. That is very fast for a plate. A sea called the Tethys lay between India and Asia. About 50 million years ago India reached Asia. Both carry light continent rock, so neither could dive under the other. The floor of the Tethys Sea was squeezed, folded and lifted. That is why sea shells lie in the rock at the top of Everest. India has not stopped. It still pushes north by 4 to 5 centimetres a year. Parts of the Himalaya rise a few millimetres every year, while rain, ice and rivers wear them down.
examples: Fossils of the same plant, Glossopteris, are found in the coal fields of India and in Africa, Australia and Antarctica.
The six-sided lava columns of St Mary's Islands near Udupi formed about 88 million years ago, when Madagascar split away.
The great Himalayan earthquakes, such as Kangra in 1905 and Nepal in 2015, happen because India is still pushing.
explanations.art: Four small globes in a row showing India joined to Africa and Antarctica, India alone in the ocean, India touching Asia, and India today with the Himalaya drawn as a crumpled line.
explanations.context: This card tells how the land you live on came to be where it is. It is the reason India has the highest mountains on Earth and some of the largest earthquakes.

perspectives.who: Geologists who read fossils and the magnetism frozen in old rocks
perspectives.explanation: Lava records the direction of the Earth's magnet when it cools. Old Indian lavas show that India once lay far south of the equator. Most studies put the first touch with Asia at 50 to 55 million years ago.

perspectives.who: Jonathan Aitchison and other geologists, in 2007
perspectives.explanation: They argue that India first hit a chain of islands, and that the true meeting of the two continents came much later, about 35 million years ago. The date is still argued.

perspectives.who: People who keep shaligram stones
perspectives.explanation: Black stones with a spiral inside are found in the Kali Gandaki river in Nepal. Many Hindus have kept them for centuries as a form of Vishnu. Geologists read the same stones as ammonites, sea animals who lived in the Tethys Sea more than 100 million years ago. One stone carries both meanings.

explanations.concept: The Deccan Traps: a flood of lava
explanations.definition: The Deccan Traps are a huge pile of basalt, which is cooled lava, covering much of western and central India. They formed in a burst of eruptions about 66 million years ago.
explanations.description: Not every volcano is a cone. About 66 million years ago, long cracks opened in the ground of India, and runny lava poured out in floods. One flow could spread for hundreds of kilometres before it cooled. Then the next flow covered it. This went on, in bursts, for several hundred thousand years. The lava pile is more than 2 kilometres thick near the Western Ghats. It still covers about half a million square kilometres, which is nearly one sixth of India. The layers have worn into steps on the hillsides. The word trap comes from a Swedish word for stairs. Over millions of years the basalt broke down into black soil, which holds water well and grows cotton and jowar. Most geologists think India was then passing over the hot spot that today feeds the volcano on Réunion island.
examples: The step-like hills at Mahabaleshwar and all along the Western Ghats in Maharashtra.
The black soil of northern Karnataka, in Belagavi, Vijayapura, Kalaburagi and Bidar, and of western Telangana.
The caves of Ajanta and Ellora, which were carved into the Deccan basalt.
explanations.art: A hillside in the Western Ghats cut into dark horizontal steps like a giant staircase, with a cotton field on black soil in front.
explanations.context: This card describes the largest volcanic event in India's history. It shows that a volcano can be a flood from cracks, and that lava later becomes soil.

perspectives.who: Geologists who follow the hot spot trail, such as Vincent Courtillot
perspectives.explanation: As India moved north, the hot spot stayed behind and left a line of volcanic ridges on the sea floor, under Lakshadweep, the Maldives and Mauritius. The trail ends at Réunion, where a volcano erupts today.

perspectives.who: Farmers of the Deccan
perspectives.explanation: For them the Traps are not a disaster of the past. They are regur, the black cotton soil. Farmers know how it swells when wet and cracks when dry, and which crops it suits. The lava is the ground of their living.

explanations.concept: Tsunami: when the sea floor moves the sea
explanations.definition: A tsunami is a set of very long waves made when a large piece of sea floor suddenly rises or drops and lifts the whole depth of the sea above it.
explanations.description: On 26 December 2004, at about half past six in the morning in India, the fault where the Indian plate dives under the Burma plate slipped. The slip ran for about 1,300 kilometres, from Sumatra to the Andaman Islands. The sea floor jumped up by several metres and pushed up all the water above it. In deep water a tsunami is less than a metre high, and ships hardly notice it. But it moves at about 700 kilometres an hour, as fast as a jet plane. Near the shore it slows down, and the water piles up into waves many metres tall. The waves reached the Nicobar Islands in minutes and the coast of Tamil Nadu about two and a half hours later. About 230,000 people died in 14 countries. More than 10,000 of them were in India. Often the sea first pulls far back from the beach. That is a warning made by the wave itself.
examples: Indira Point, the southern tip of India in the Nicobar Islands, sank by about 4 metres in the 2004 earthquake.
Since 2007, the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre in Hyderabad watches the Indian Ocean all day and all night.
The earthquake was magnitude 9.1, the third largest ever recorded.
explanations.art: A side view from Sumatra to Chennai: a step jumping up in the sea floor, a low fast wave crossing the deep ocean, and the wave rising tall as the sea gets shallow near a beach with palm trees.
explanations.context: This card explains how an earthquake under the sea makes a tsunami, using the day India can never forget. It tells you the sign to act on at a beach.

perspectives.who: The people of Simeulue island, Indonesia, and the Onge and Jarawa of the Andaman Islands
perspectives.explanation: Simeulue was close to the earthquake of 2004. Its people had a word, smong, and songs from a tsunami in 1907. The songs say that when the ground shakes hard and the sea pulls back, you must run to the hills. Nearly everyone ran, and only seven of about 78,000 people died. Reports say the Onge and the Jarawa also moved to high ground in time.

perspectives.who: Scientists at warning centres, such as the one at INCOIS in Hyderabad
perspectives.explanation: Seismographs find the earthquake within minutes. Pressure sensors on the deep sea floor feel the wave pass over them. Computers work out when it will reach each coast. In 2004 the Indian Ocean had no such system. People near the earthquake still have only minutes, so the old knowledge and the new system are both needed.

explanations.concept: What can we know before the ground shakes?
explanations.description: Here is what we know so far. Nobody can say the day, the place and the size of an earthquake before it happens. Many people have tried for more than a hundred years, and no method has worked reliably. Scientists can do three other things. They can forecast. From old earthquakes and from the measured squeeze on the rocks, they can say that a region is likely to have a large earthquake some time in the coming decades. India's earthquake map is made this way. It puts the Himalaya, the Northeast, Kutch and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands in the highest danger zones. Much of South India is in lower zones, but lower does not mean zero. They can also warn. Sensors near the fault catch the first fast waves and send a message that outruns the slower, stronger waves. That gives people a few seconds to a minute. And engineers can build so that buildings bend and do not fall. What is missing is the reason one small slip stops and another grows into a giant. Nobody knows that yet.
examples: A forecast: 'This region is likely to have a strong earthquake within the next 50 years.'
A warning: a phone alert that arrives 20 seconds before strong shaking.
A prediction nobody can honestly make: 'An earthquake will strike this town next Tuesday.'
explanations.art: Three panels: a map of India shaded by earthquake danger, a phone showing an alert with a countdown of seconds, and a calendar page with a question mark on it.
explanations.context: This card is the honest answer to the question every child asks: can we know when an earthquake is coming? It separates what is known from what is not.

perspectives.who: Robert Geller and other seismologists, writing in 1997
perspectives.explanation: They argue that earthquakes cannot be predicted at all. A fault is always close to slipping, and tiny differences nobody can measure decide when a slip starts and how far it runs. They say money is better spent on strong buildings.

perspectives.who: Chinese scientists at Haicheng in 1975
perspectives.explanation: After many small earthquakes and reports of odd changes in wells, officials moved people out of their homes. A magnitude 7.3 earthquake struck hours later, and many lives were saved. But the next year an even deadlier earthquake at Tangshan came with no such signs, and nobody was warned.

perspectives.who: Scientists who track animals, such as Martin Wikelski
perspectives.explanation: In 2020 his team reported that cows, sheep and dogs on a farm in Italy moved about more in the hours before nearby earthquakes. Other scientists say the study was small and the pattern must be tested in many more places.

agreed.text: Satellite markers fixed to rock on every continent move a few centimetres each year, and the directions match the plate map.
agreed.evidence: Thousands of ground stations, including many across India, have recorded their own positions every day since the 1990s.

agreed.text: The floor of the open ocean is young. Almost none of it is older than 200 million years, while some land rocks are 4,000 million years old.
agreed.evidence: Ships have drilled and dated sea floor rock since 1968. It is youngest at the ridges and older on both sides, in matching stripes.

agreed.text: A great earthquake makes the whole Earth ring like a struck bell.
agreed.evidence: After the earthquake of 26 December 2004, seismographs all over the world showed the ground everywhere moving by about a centimetre, and the ringing lasted for weeks.

agreed.text: About half of the heat flowing out of the Earth is made by atoms breaking apart in the rock.
agreed.evidence: Detectors in Japan and Italy have counted tiny particles called neutrinos that come up from these atoms inside the Earth.

agreed.text: The Deccan lava erupted very close to the time the giant dinosaurs died out, about 66 million years ago.
agreed.evidence: Two teams dated the lava layers in 2019 with two different methods. Both placed the main eruptions within a few hundred thousand years of the die-off.

agreed.text: People can set off earthquakes by filling large dams, pumping water into deep rock, or mining.
agreed.evidence: At Koyna in Maharashtra, earthquakes began soon after the dam was filled in 1962 and still rise and fall with the water level. One in 1967 was magnitude 6.3.

challenging.claim: The Deccan eruptions, and not only an asteroid, ended the giant dinosaurs.
challenging.who: Gerta Keller of Princeton University and geologists who work with her in India
challenging.for: The eruptions poured out gases that could heat the air, then cool it, and make the sea acid. Fossils in some places show sea life already in trouble before the asteroid fell.
challenging.against: A layer of asteroid dust lies around the whole world at exactly that age, and the crater is in Mexico. A large study in 2020 found that the main die-off matches the asteroid, with the lava playing a smaller part.
challenging.context: This card gives a live argument among scientists about India's own lava. It shows that a famous story can still be open.

challenging.claim: Animals sense an earthquake hours before it comes.
challenging.who: Martin Wikelski and his team, and many people's own stories from Bhuj, Latur and the 2004 tsunami
challenging.for: Tagged farm animals in Italy grew restless before earthquakes that were close by. Many animals feel faint shaking and smell gases that humans miss, so a real signal is possible.
challenging.against: A review of 180 published studies in 2018 found that most reports were stories told afterwards, with no record of how the animals behaved on ordinary days. Animals grow restless for many reasons.
challenging.context: This card looks at an old belief that scientists are now testing with tags and numbers. It is a good one to design your own test for.

challenging.claim: Hot spots are fed by plumes of hot rock rising from the bottom of the mantle.
challenging.who: W. Jason Morgan, who proposed it in 1971
challenging.for: It explains chains of islands that get older in a line, such as Hawaii, and the trail from the Deccan to Réunion. Earthquake waves show slow, hot rock deep under some hot spots.
challenging.against: Gillian Foulger and others point out that under many hot spots no deep column is found, and some chains do not age in a neat line. They say cracks in a stretched plate can explain them.
challenging.context: This card is about volcanoes far from plate edges. Most geologists accept plumes, but a serious group does not.

challenging.claim: Mangrove forests shielded villages from the 2004 tsunami.
challenging.who: K. Kathiresan and N. Rajendran, who studied 18 villages near Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu in 2005
challenging.for: Villages behind thick mangroves lost fewer lives and less property than villages on open shore nearby. The tangled roots and trunks slow moving water.
challenging.against: Alexander Kerr and Andrew Baird looked at the same numbers again. They found that a village's height above the sea and its distance from the shore explained most of the difference. Against the largest waves, trees may do little.
challenging.context: This card asks how much a forest can protect a coast. The answer matters for every fishing village, and scientists still disagree about the size of the effect.

challenging.claim: The mantle is a sea of melted rock, and the plates float on it like boats.
challenging.who: Many drawings, films and older school books
challenging.for: Lava comes out of volcanoes, so it is easy to think there is lava everywhere underneath. Drawings often colour the mantle bright orange and red.
challenging.against: S waves pass through the mantle, and they do not pass through liquids. So the mantle is solid. It only creeps, and magma is made in a few small regions.
challenging.context: This card names a very common picture of the inside of the Earth and gives the evidence that it is wrong.

challenging.claim: Someone can tell you the day an earthquake will strike.
challenging.who: Astrologers, some messages passed around on phones, and a few scientists over the years
challenging.for: At Haicheng in China in 1975, people were moved out hours before a large earthquake, and it looked as if prediction had arrived.
challenging.against: No method has worked a second time. Tangshan in 1976, Bhuj in 2001 and Sumatra in 2004 all came without warning. When predictions are checked against records, they do no better than guessing.
challenging.context: This card deals with a claim that returns after every earthquake. It helps a family know which messages to ignore.

big_questions.q: The floor feels perfectly still, and instruments say it is moving. Which one is true, and how would you decide?
big_questions.hint: Think about a clock's hour hand. Does it move? How do you know?

big_questions.q: The mantle is solid in one second and flows over a million years. So what do the words solid and liquid really mean?
big_questions.hint: Think of honey from the fridge, wet sand, and a ball of dough left on a plate overnight.

big_questions.q: We know an earthquake will come to the Himalaya, but not when. How should people live with something that is certain and unknown at once?
big_questions.hint: Think of other things in your life that are sure to happen on a day nobody knows.

big_questions.q: The same lava that buried the land became the black soil that feeds people. Is a volcano good or bad?
big_questions.hint: Ask who is answering, and when: a deer on that day, or a farmer 60 million years later.

big_questions.q: Nobody has ever seen the Earth's core. How sure can we be about a thing we know only through waves?
big_questions.hint: Think of how you know what is inside a wrapped gift when you shake it.

big_questions.q: If the plates stopped moving, there would be no earthquakes. Would the Earth be a better home for life, or a worse one?
big_questions.hint: Think about where mountains, rivers, fresh soil and the gases of the air come from.

big_questions.q: The people of Simeulue were saved by a song. Is a song knowledge in the same way that a seismograph reading is?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each one remembers, how long it lasts, and who can use it.

story.title: The Night the Needle Moved
story.note: A made-up story. Meenu, Kaveri, Imran and Thatha are imagined, and so is this earthquake. The place is real: the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre in Hyderabad has watched the Indian Ocean day and night since 2007. The science is real too. Waves from an earthquake near the Nicobar Islands take about four minutes to reach Hyderabad, and an earthquake whose fault slips sideways lifts very little water.
text: Meenu was nine, and she was meant to be asleep on the sofa at the back of the big room.

Her aunt Kaveri worked nights in Hyderabad, in a room full of screens that watched the Indian Ocean. Tonight there was nobody at home to stay with Meenu, so she had come along with a pillow and a book.

The room was quiet. On the largest screen, thin lines ran from left to right, one line for each seismograph. There was a line for Port Blair, a line for Chennai, a line for Hyderabad itself. All of them were nearly flat.
'Each line is the ground at one place,' Kaveri had told her. 'When the ground is quiet, the line is quiet.'
A young man called Imran sat at the next desk. It was his second week. Kaveri was teaching him the work, and he wrote everything she said in a small notebook.
At seven minutes past two, the line for Port Blair jumped.
It did not wiggle. It leapt into tall, crowded zigzags that filled its whole strip. A soft alarm began to sound. Kaveri put down her tea.
'Where?' said Imran.
'Wait,' said Kaveri. 'Watch the other lines. The waves will tell us.'
Meenu sat up. The line for Chennai was still flat. The line for Hyderabad was still flat. She put her hand on the floor. It felt just as it always felt.
Then the Chennai line jumped. And a little after that, about four minutes after the first alarm, the Hyderabad line began to shake too.
Meenu stared at it. That line was this building. That line was the floor under her hand. The ground beneath her was moving, right now, and she felt nothing at all.
'Near the Nicobar Islands,' said Kaveri, reading the screen. 'About two thousand kilometres from us. Magnitude 7.6. It is under the sea.'
Imran had gone pale. 'Under the sea. So a tsunami is coming.'
'We do not know that yet,' said Kaveri. 'Tell me what we need to find out.'
He looked at his notebook. 'If the sea floor went up or down.'

'Yes. A tsunami is not made by shaking. It is made when the sea floor lifts the water. If the two sides of the fault only slid past each other, sideways, the water above stays where it is.' She was already typing. 'The first waves say this one slid mostly sideways. But I will not trust one sign. There is a pressure sensor on the sea floor west of the Nicobars. If a wave is crossing the ocean, the sensor will feel the extra water pass over it.'

They waited. Meenu had never seen grown-ups wait like that. Nobody spoke. On the coast of Tamil Nadu, her grandfather was asleep in his house two streets from the beach at Nagapattinam. Thatha had lost his boat and two of his friends to the sea in 2004. He did not like to talk about that day.
A new line appeared on Kaveri's screen. It rose by a tiny amount and came down again.

'Three centimetres,' said Kaveri, and she let out a long breath. 'A wave of three centimetres in the open sea. That will harm nobody. We send the message: earthquake recorded, no tsunami threat to India.'
Imran sent it. His hands were not quite steady.
Later, when the alarm was off and fresh tea had come, he asked the question Meenu wanted to ask. 'Madam, could we have known? Yesterday, I mean. That it would happen tonight.'

'No,' said Kaveri. 'Nobody could. We know that the Indian plate is diving under those islands, about four centimetres every year. We know the rock there is being bent. We can say that the place will break again and again. We cannot say the night. I have done this work for fifteen years and I still cannot. What we can do is be awake when it happens.'
Meenu looked at the Hyderabad line. It had gone flat again.
'Athai,' she said, 'the floor really moved? Here?'

'By less than the width of a hair. But yes. The rock under the Nicobars and the rock under this sofa are one rock, Meenu. When it breaks there, it trembles here. The line only shows us what our bodies are too slow and too large to notice.'
In the morning Meenu rang her grandfather before he could hear the news from anyone else.
'Thatha, there was an earthquake in the night near the Nicobars. A big one. But the sea floor slid sideways. It did not lift the sea. So there is no wave. I watched them check.'
He was silent for a moment. 'It slid sideways,' he said slowly. 'In all these years nobody told me there were two kinds.' Then he asked, 'And how did you know before my radio did?'
'Because the floor in Hyderabad shook,' said Meenu. 'I had my hand on it. I just could not feel it.'

After the call she sat on the steps outside and pressed both palms flat on the warm stone. It felt completely still. She kept her hands there for a long time, wondering what else was moving that she had always called still.
story.epiphany: Meenu's own floor moved with an earthquake two thousand kilometres away, and her hand felt nothing. The ground that seems separate and still is one connected rock, and it is always carrying some movement that we are too slow to feel.
ask: Meenu felt nothing, and the line showed the floor moving. Which would you trust, your hand or the line? Why?
Kaveri could not say which night the earthquake would come, but she was ready when it did. Is being ready a kind of knowing?
What else around you might be moving that you have always called still?
art: A dim control room at night with a wall of screens showing flat lines, a woman at a desk with a steel tumbler of tea, a young man with a notebook, and a girl sitting up on a sofa at the back with a pillow.
A close view of a screen where the top line has leapt into tall zigzags while the two lines below are still flat, and a girl's hand pressed flat on the floor.
A side view of the sea west of small islands, with a small sensor on the deep sea floor and a very low, long wave passing far above it.
A girl sitting on stone steps in morning light with both palms pressed on the step, a phone beside her.

roots.context: You have pulled a box that sat still and then jumped, and you have followed India across an ocean. Now we ask what a moving ground tells us about stillness, about ourselves and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Sticking Box test, your hand never stopped pulling, yet the box sat still and then jumped. The quiet wait and the jump were one movement. The ground under you is like that box. It is being carried and squeezed right now, by a few centimetres a year. An earthquake is the last second of a hundred quiet years.
deep_truth.habit: We sort the world into still things and moving things. We call the ground solid and an earthquake sudden. That sorting comes from the length of our lives and the speed of our eyes. It does not come from the Earth.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Sticking Box test the rubber band stretched all through the wait, so the jump was being prepared the whole time. Satellite markers show India moving about 5 centimetres every year. Sea shells lie in the rock at the top of Everest.

three.who_am_i: The iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones came out of rock that volcanoes brought up and rivers ground down. You are a piece of the moving Earth that can stand up, look around and ask questions about the rest.
three.what_is_life: Volcanoes gave the early Earth much of its air. Moving plates keep lifting fresh rock, and rain washes its minerals into soil and sea. Life and the restless ground have shaped each other for thousands of millions of years.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is a slow movement, and the things in it are that movement seen at one moment. A mountain is a wave of rock that takes fifty million years to rise and fall.

roots.thread: Follow one push. Heat deep in the Earth moves the mantle. The mantle and the sinking sea floor move the plates. The Indian plate carried a piece of Gondwana across an ocean, poured out the Deccan lava on the way, and lifted a sea floor into the Himalaya. The Himalaya make the rivers, the rivers make the plains, and the plains grow the rice on your plate. The same push broke the rock at Bhuj and lifted the sea in 2004. You cannot keep the parts you like and remove the parts you fear, because they are one movement. Consciousness is the ground that all of this arises in, and the rock, the river, the rice and the child who eats it are the same world showing up in different forms.

teachings.teaching: It moves, and it moves not. It is far, and it is near. It is inside all this, and it is outside all this.
teachings.link: The sage says that moving and not moving can both be true of one thing. The floor under you is like this: at rest to your hand, travelling to a satellite.

teachings.teaching: All things that are put together are impermanent. One who sees this with wisdom grows weary of suffering. This is the path to purity.
teachings.link: The Buddha taught that nothing made of parts stays as it is. A mountain range is put together by a collision and taken apart by rain. Even the Himalaya are an event.

teachings.source: Heraclitus of Ephesus, as reported in Plato's Cratylus 402a
teachings.teaching: Everything moves on and nothing stays at rest. You could not step twice into the same river.
teachings.link: Heraclitus chose a river because its movement is easy to see. Plate science says the same of the river bank, the bed rock and the continent, at a speed too slow for the eye.

science.text: No place on the Earth's surface is fixed. Every continent and every piece of sea floor is moving, and satellites measure the movement every day.

James Lovelock and Lynn Margulis proposed in 1974 that living beings, air, sea and rock work together as one system that keeps the Earth fit for life. They called it Gaia. Scientists accept that life and rock change each other, and they argue about whether the whole can be called one living system.

Some scientists think moving plates are needed for a planet to keep life going over a very long time, because plates recycle the materials life uses. Only one planet with life is known, so this cannot be checked yet.

other_view.who: Most geologists, and the philosophers called physicalists
other_view.view: Plates are rock moved by heat and weight, and nothing more is needed to explain them. Still and moving are only words for slow and fast. The rock has no awareness, and the Earth is not one being. The feeling that it all hangs together is a feeling in a human brain, and it is not a fact about the planet.

practice.title: Standing on the moving ground
practice.say: Stand with bare feet on the floor and let your arms hang. Feel your weight press down through your heels and your toes. Close your eyes and breathe slowly five times. The floor feels still. Now remember that this floor, this building and this whole land are travelling north-east. They move about as fast as your fingernails grow. Stay with both things at once for five more breaths. Then open your eyes.
practice.kid: Stand with bare feet on the floor. Feel your weight in your feet. Close your eyes and breathe slowly five times. The floor feels still, and it is also travelling. Hold both ideas for five more breaths.

ask: If the ground is always moving, is there anything at all that is truly still? How would you look for it?
The push that makes the earthquake also makes the mountain, the river and the rice. Can you want one without the other?
Your bones were once rock. Where does the Earth end and where do you begin?
roots.art: A child standing barefoot with eyes closed on a floor that is drawn as the top of a very thick slab of layered rock, with a faint arrow under the slab pointing north-east and snow mountains far behind.

games.title: Ride the Indian Plate: a race from Gondwana to today
games.context: This is a board game for 2 to 4 players. Each player is a piece of the Indian plate, travelling from the old southern land of Gondwana to where India is today. The squares are real events, in the order they happened.

setup.art: A long sheet of paper with a winding track of 24 numbered squares drawn on it, starting near a shape marked Gondwana and ending at a map of India.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a track of 24 squares on a large sheet. Copy the words for each square.

setup.art: Twelve small paper cards in a pile beside the track, with a die and three buttons of different colours.
setup.caption: 2. Cut out the 12 question cards. Put them in a pile with the questions facing up.

setup.art: Two children and a parent round the board, one child holding a card and reading its question aloud.
setup.caption: 3. Roll, move and do what your square says. The first to reach square 24 wins.

printables.title: 24 squares on a winding track
items: 1. START. 180 million years ago. India is locked inside the great southern land of Gondwana, beside Africa, Antarctica and Australia.
2. Hot rock rises under Gondwana and the land begins to crack. Roll again.
4. 130 million years ago. India and Madagascar break away together from Antarctica and Australia. Move ahead 1.
5. New sea floor is being made behind you at a spreading ridge. Stay here.
7. 88 million years ago. Madagascar splits from India. Lava cools into six-sided columns at St Mary's Islands near Udupi. Miss a turn to look at them.
8. India is now an island continent, alone in the ocean. Stay here.
9. The old sea floor in front of you is diving under Asia and pulling you along. You speed up to 15 centimetres a year. Move ahead 2.
11. 66 million years ago. Cracks open and the Deccan lava floods begin. Miss a turn while the lava flows.
12. Flow upon flow of lava builds the stepped hills of the Western Ghats. Go back 1 to look at them.
14. The hot spot stays behind as you move on. It leaves a trail under Lakshadweep, the Maldives and Mauritius. Move ahead 1.
15. The Tethys Sea between you and Asia is getting narrow. Ammonites swim in it. Stay here.
17. About 50 million years ago. India touches Asia. Neither can dive. From now on, move only half of what you roll, rounded up.
18. The floor of the Tethys Sea is squeezed and lifted. Sea shells begin their ride to the mountain tops. Move ahead 1.
20. The Himalaya rise a few millimetres a year. Rain and ice wear them down, and rivers carry the sand south to build the great plains. Stay here.
21. The plate edge sticks, then slips. Shillong 1897, Kangra 1905, Bihar and Nepal 1934, Assam 1950. Miss a turn.
23. Bhuj, 26 January 2001. Sumatra and the Andamans, 26 December 2004. An old crack inside the plate slips, and then the plate's eastern edge. Go back 1.
24. TODAY. You are still moving north-east, about 5 centimetres a year. The first player to arrive wins, but the journey has not ended.

printables.title: 12 two-sided question cards, with the question on the front and the answer on the back

items.f: Why are sea shells and ammonites found in rock high in the Himalaya?
items.b: The rock was once the floor of the Tethys Sea. It was squeezed and lifted when India pushed into Asia.

items.f: A plate moves 5 centimetres every year. How far does it move in 20 years?
items.b: 100 centimetres, which is 1 metre. 5 times 20 is 100.

items.f: The mantle is solid rock. How can a solid carry a plate along?
items.b: Hot solid rock creeps very slowly, like stiff dough. A quick knock breaks it. A push that lasts a million years bends it.

items.f: DEFEND. Which did more to end the giant dinosaurs: the asteroid or the Deccan lava? Give one reason.
items.b: Scientists still argue about this. Any answer with a reason earns the move.

items.f: You are on a beach. The ground shakes for a long time. Then the sea pulls far back. What do you do?
items.b: Leave at once for high ground or go far inland, and tell others. Do not wait, and do not go to look.

items.f: Bhuj is about 400 kilometres from the edge of the Indian plate. Why did it shake in 2001?
items.b: India is squeezed as it pushes into Asia. An old crack deep inside the plate slipped under that squeeze.

items.f: S waves from earthquakes do not pass through the outer core. What does that tell us about it?
items.b: It is liquid. S waves shake rock from side to side, and a liquid does not spring back sideways.

items.f: DEFEND. Is a volcano a destroyer or a maker? Give one example.
items.b: It buries land, and it builds islands and soil. Any answer with a real example earns the move.

items.f: Why are there so many volcanoes around the edge of the Pacific Ocean?
items.b: Sea floor dives under other plates all round the Pacific. Water carried down helps rock to melt, and the magma rises.

items.f: Can scientists name the day an earthquake will strike? What can they say?
items.b: No. They can say which regions are likely to shake hard some day. They can also send a warning seconds after an earthquake begins.

items.f: Barren Island has an active volcano. Chennai has none. Why?
items.b: Barren Island sits above the place where the Indian plate dives under the Burma plate. Chennai sits far inside its plate.

items.f: DEFEND. Is the ground under you still or moving? Give your evidence.
items.b: Both can be defended. It feels still. Satellites show it moving a few centimetres a year. Any answer with evidence earns the move.

rules: You need the board, the 12 question cards, one die from any board game, and a button or coin for each player. Two players is enough.
Put every button on square 1. Stack the cards with the questions facing up, so that nobody sees the answers.
On your turn, roll the die and move that many squares. Then read your square aloud and do what it says. You follow only the square you land on by rolling, not a square you are sent to.

On a QUESTION square, the player on your left takes the top card and reads the question to you. Answer aloud. Then the card is turned over and the answer is read. If your answer matches, move ahead 1 square. The card goes to the bottom of the pile.
On a DEFEND card there is no single right answer. Give your view and one reason or piece of evidence. If the other players agree that you gave a real reason, move ahead 1 square.
Once you have landed on or passed square 17, you move only half of each roll, rounded up. A roll of 5 moves you 3. This is because India slowed down when it met Asia.
The first player to reach square 24 wins. You do not need an exact roll to finish. Play on to see who comes second, if you like.

flow.do: Draw a winding track of 24 squares on the back of an old calendar or two sheets taped together. Copy the words for each square, or write only the number and keep the list beside you. Cut out the 12 cards. Find a die and a button for each player.
flow.say: This track is the real journey of the land we live on. Square 1 is 180 million years ago. Square 24 is today. Before we play, guess how many of those years India spent as an island.
flow.kid: Draw a track of 24 squares. Cut out the 12 cards. Put your button on square 1.
flow.parent: A grown-up handles the cutting. To save time, number the squares and read each one from the list as it is landed on. The answer to the island question is about 40 million years, from 88 million to about 50 million years ago.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ride the Indian Plate. You make the board and the cards.

flow.do: Play until someone passes square 12. Read every square aloud as it is landed on. On each QUESTION square, let the player answer fully before the card is turned over.
flow.say: Roll and move. Read your square to everyone. If it is a question, think aloud before you answer. A reason counts for more than a fast answer.
flow.kid: Roll the die and move. Read your square aloud. Do what it says.

ask.q: At square 9 the plate speeds up. What is pulling it?
good: The old sea floor diving under Asia.
The heavy edge sinking into the mantle.

flow.parent: If an answer is close to the card but in the child's own words, count it as right. If it is wrong, read the card's answer once and move on without comment. The card will come round again.
flow.context: In this step you play the first half of the journey, from Gondwana to the Deccan lava.

flow.do: Play on to the end. Remind players of the half-roll rule after square 17. The first to reach square 24 wins.
flow.say: India has met Asia now. Everyone past square 17 moves only half a roll. Why would a plate slow down when it meets another continent?
flow.kid: After square 17, move only half your roll. Reach square 24 to win.

check.q: Why did India slow down after it met Asia?
options: Two continents met and neither could dive under
The mantle cooled and went hard
India ran out of sea to cross
check.why: Continent rock is too light to sink into the mantle, so the two lands jammed and crumpled into the Himalaya. The mantle did not go hard. If you chose the sea, remember that the plate is moved by forces in the rock and not by the water.

flow.parent: With 4 players the cards may go round twice, which is fine. A player who misses a turn still listens to the other squares being read.
flow.context: In this step you play the second half, from the meeting with Asia to today.

flow.do: After the game, lay the three DEFEND cards on the table. Each player chooses one and gives a view with a reason, even if they gave one during the game.
flow.say: These three cards have no answer on the back. Choose one and tell us what you think and why. Then listen to one person who thinks differently.
flow.kid: Choose one DEFEND card. Say what you think and why. Listen to another view.
flow.think: The game ends at square 24, but India is still moving. What would you write on square 25?
flow.parent: There is no winner in this step. Notice if your child uses evidence from the game, the experiment or the explanation cards. Ask what would change their mind.
flow.context: In this step you talk about the three questions that have more than one good answer.

experiments.title: The Sticking Box: can you tell when it will jump?
experiments.question: If you pull a heavy box with a slow, steady pull on a rubber band, does the box move steadily? Can you tell when it will move next?
experiments.predict: Before you pull, guess. Will the box glide along with your hand, or will it wait and then jump? Will every wait be the same length? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The same box, the same rubber bands, the same cloth and the same slow pull of 1 centimetre for each count are used all the way through. Only the weight in the box changes: one packet in Round 1 and two packets in Round 2. Each round goes on for 8 jumps, because one jump alone can be a fluke.

materials.item: a shoe box, or a plastic or steel box with a lid, about the size of a brick
packets of the same weight to put inside: rice, dal, atta or sugar, 500 grams or 1 kilogram each
rubber bands of the same kind, looped together into a short chain
string, about 1 metre, to tie round the box like a parcel
a cotton bedsheet, dhurrie, towel or yoga mat, spread flat on the floor
a tailor's measuring tape, or a strip of newspaper marked in centimetres with a ruler, about 150 centimetres long
paper and a pencil for the results table

experiments.safety: A stretched rubber band can snap back. Pull low along the floor and keep faces away from the line of the band. If the band stretches to three times its slack length and the box has still not moved, stop. Use a thicker band, or two bands side by side.
experiments.record: Fill in one row of the table for each jump, 8 rows for each round. Then write three lines: what I thought, what I saw, and why I think it happened.
experiments.context: In this experiment you pull a weighted box with a rubber band, slowly and steadily. The box stands for a stuck fault, the band for rock that bends, and your hand for a plate that never stops. You find out if the jumps can be told in advance.

setup.art: A shoe box tied round with string like a parcel, with a chain of two rubber bands looped onto the string at the front.
setup.caption: 1. Put one packet in the box. Tie string round it. Loop the rubber-band chain onto the string at the front.

setup.art: The box on a bedsheet spread on the floor, with a measuring tape laid beside it and the front of the box at the zero mark.
setup.caption: 2. Lay the tape beside the cloth. Put the front of the box at 0.

setup.art: A child's hand low on the floor pulling the end of the rubber band along the tape, while the band is stretched and the box has not moved.
setup.caption: 3. Pull the band 1 centimetre for each count. Keep counting until the box jumps.

setup.art: A parent pointing at where the front of the box now sits on the tape, and a table on paper with numbers being written in.
setup.caption: 4. Write the count and the new place of the box. Start counting again from 1.

flow.do: Show your child the box, the rubber bands and the cloth. Say that you will pull the band very slowly and steadily. Write down the guess and the reason before anything is pulled.
flow.say: I will pull this band slowly, 1 centimetre at a time, and never stop. Will the box glide along with my hand? Or will it wait and jump? Will every wait be the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A hand will pull the band slowly and never stop. Guess what the box will do. Say why you think so.

ask.q: What is holding the box back when the band first pulls?
good: The cloth grips the bottom of the box.
Its weight presses it onto the cloth.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say the box will slide smoothly because the pull is smooth. Write the guess and the reason at the top of the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sticking Box. You guess before you pull.

flow.do: Put one packet in the box and close it. Tie the string round the box like a parcel. To make the chain, push one band halfway through the other. Pass it through its own loop and pull tight. Loop the chain onto the string at the front. Spread the cloth flat and lay the tape beside it. Put the front of the box at 0.
flow.say: The box is a patch of rock that is stuck. The band is rock that can bend and store energy. My hand is the plate, and a plate never stops. Try one pull to see that the band holds.
flow.kid: Put one packet in the box. Tie the string round it. Hook on the rubber bands. Put the front of the box at 0.
flow.parent: You need about 1.5 metres of clear floor. Hold the cloth flat with your feet or with books on its corners, so that only the box can move. Do one trial pull. The box should stay put while the band stretches, then jerk forward by 2 to 10 centimetres. If it glides without jumping, add the second packet or use a rougher cloth such as a towel. If the band becomes thin and pale before the box moves, use two bands side by side.
flow.context: In this step you build the model fault and check that it sticks and slips.

flow.do: Round 1. Your child hooks one finger in the end of the band and rests that hand on the floor. The hand moves 1 centimetre along the tape for each count, about one count a second. Count aloud. When the box jumps, write the count and the place of the front of the box. Start again from 1. Go on for 8 jumps.
flow.say: Move your hand one centimetre for each count. Do not speed up and do not stop. Keep counting. When the box jumps, I will write your count and where the box is now. Then start again from one.
flow.kid: Pull 1 centimetre for each count. Count aloud. When the box jumps, say your count. Then start again from 1.

ask.q: Were the waits all the same? Were the jumps all the same size?
good: Some jumps were small and some were big.
They were close to each other but not the same.

flow.parent: With one 1 kilogram packet on a cotton sheet, waits of about 6 to 15 counts and jumps of 3 to 10 centimetres are typical. Yours will differ, so write what you see. A tiny shuffle of under 1 centimetre still counts as a jump. Write it down, because real faults have small slips too. Work out each jump size by taking away the box's last place from its new place. With 2 to 4 children, share the jobs: puller, counter, box watcher and writer.
flow.context: In this step you pull with one packet in the box and record 8 jumps.

flow.do: Round 2. Put the second packet in the box and start again from 0. Pull in the same way for 8 jumps. This time your child also calls 'now' one count before the jump is expected. Put a tick in the margin for each call that was right.
flow.say: Now the box is twice as heavy. Pull just as before. This time, try to call 'now' one count before it jumps. You have watched 8 jumps already, so use what you learned.
flow.kid: Add the second packet. Pull as before. Call 'now' just before you think it will jump.

ask.q: How did the heavier box change the waits and the jumps?
good: The band stretched further before the box moved.

check.q: During a wait, the box is not moving. Where is the energy of your pull going?
check.why: Your hand moves, so you are doing work, and the band stores it as it stretches. If you chose 'nowhere', look at the band during the next wait. It gets longer with every count, and all of that is let go in the jump.

flow.parent: A heavier box presses harder on the cloth, so the band must stretch further before it wins. Most families see longer waits and bigger jumps. Most children get only one or two calls right out of 8, and some get none. That is the result. Do not help them to do better.
flow.context: In this step you change one thing, the weight, and you try to call each jump before it happens.

flow.do: Look at the two columns of waits together. Find the shortest and the longest wait in each round. Ask your child to write what they thought, what they saw and why. Only then talk about real faults.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did the table show? Why do you think the box behaved like that? Then tell me this. What could you say about the next jump, and what could you not say?
flow.kid: Look at your table. Find the shortest wait and the longest wait. Write what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: You could watch the rubber band stretch. Nobody can see the rock stretch 20 kilometres down. What could scientists measure from the surface instead?
flow.parent: A good answer says the pull was steady but the box moved in jumps, because friction held it until the band pulled hard enough. It says the waits were roughly alike but never exactly the same. So you could say 'it will jump again, in about 10 counts', but not 'it will jump on count 10'. After your child has said this, give the link. Seismologists can say a fault will slip again, and roughly how often. They cannot say the day. Then say what the model leaves out. A real fault is kilometres deep, nobody can see how stretched it is, and one slip can set off the fault next to it. So real earthquakes are far less regular than your box.
flow.context: In this step you say what the results show, and you compare your box with a real fault.

experiments.title: Runny or sticky: which one traps the bubbles?
experiments.question: When air is blown into a runny liquid and into a thick, sticky one, which lets the bubbles out faster? Which one builds the steeper hill when it is poured?
experiments.predict: Guess before you blow. In which tumbler will the bubbles be bigger? In which will they last longer after you stop? Which liquid will make the taller heap on a plate? Give a reason for each guess.
experiments.fair_test: Both tumblers are the same size and are filled to the same height. The same person blows through the same kind of straw, gently, for a slow count of 5. One tablespoon of each liquid is poured from the same height onto the same kind of plate. Only the liquid changes. Each test is done three times.
results_table: Seconds until the bubbles are gone

materials.item: steel tumblers of the same size
water
atta or besan, stirred with the same amount of water into a thick, smooth batter
materials.qty: 6 tablespoons of flour and 6 of water

materials.item: drinking straws, one for each liquid
flat steel plates
a tablespoon, a ruler and a clock or phone that shows seconds

experiments.record: Fill in the table for water and for batter. Draw the two heaps from the side. Then write what you thought, what you saw and why.
experiments.context: In this experiment you blow bubbles into water and into thick batter, and you pour a spoonful of each. Magma can be runny or sticky in the same way. You find out what that difference does to the bubbles and to the shape of the heap.

setup.art: Two steel tumblers side by side, one half full of water and one half full of thick pale batter, each with a straw standing in it.
setup.caption: 1. Half fill one tumbler with water and the other with thick batter.

setup.art: A child blowing gently through a straw into the batter, with one large dome-shaped bubble rising at the surface.
setup.caption: 2. Blow gently for a count of 5. Watch the bubbles and time how long they last.

setup.art: Two steel plates seen from the side: a wide, flat puddle of water on one and a rounded heap of batter on the other, with a ruler beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Pour one tablespoon of each onto a plate. Measure how wide it spreads.

flow.do: Stir 6 tablespoons of atta or besan with 6 tablespoons of water until smooth. It should drop slowly off the spoon. Half fill one tumbler with it and the other with water. Ask for the three guesses and write them down with the reasons.
flow.say: One liquid is runny and one is sticky. I will blow air into each. Where will the bubbles be bigger? Where will they last longer? Which will make a taller heap on a plate? Tell me why.
flow.kid: Mix the flour and water until smooth. Half fill both tumblers. Make your three guesses and give reasons.
flow.parent: If the batter runs off the spoon like milk, add a spoon of flour. If it will not drop at all, add a spoon of water. Do not explain anything about volcanoes yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of Runny or Sticky. You make the two liquids and guess.

flow.do: Put a straw to the bottom of the water. Blow gently for a slow count of 5, then stop. Time how long the bubbles take to vanish. Do the same in the batter with the other straw. Do each one three times and write the results.
flow.say: Blow gently, the same each time, and never suck. Watch the size of the bubbles. Listen to them. When you stop, I will time how long they stay.
flow.kid: Blow gently for a count of 5. Never suck. Watch the bubbles and listen. Count how long they stay.

ask.q: What was different about the bubbles in the batter?
good: They rose slowly and burst with a plop.
Some stayed in the batter after I stopped.

check.q: In which liquid did the air find it harder to get out?
options: It was the same in both
check.why: A thick liquid flows slowly, so it closes in around a bubble and holds it. The bubble must grow large before it can push its way up. If you chose water, watch again and time how long the bubbles stay after you stop blowing.

flow.parent: In water the bubbles are small, rise at once and are gone in about a second. In batter the air collects into large bubbles that push the surface up into a dome and burst with a plop, sometimes throwing specks. Some stay trapped for many seconds. Blowing hard into the water makes it splash, which spoils the test, so keep the breath gentle. Keep the tumblers on a plate to catch drips.
flow.context: In this step you blow the same gentle breath into both liquids and compare the bubbles.
