flow.do: Hold a level tablespoon of water 2 centimetres above the middle of one plate and tip it out. Do the same with batter on the other plate. Wait 30 seconds. Measure the width of each puddle and look at both from the side.
flow.say: Now we pour. One spoon of each, from the same height. Wait for thirty counts. Which has spread wider? Which stands taller? Bend down and look from the side.
flow.kid: Pour one spoon of each on a plate. Wait 30 seconds. Measure how wide each one spread.
flow.parent: The water runs out into a wide, very thin sheet, often 10 centimetres or more across. The batter makes a heap only 4 to 6 centimetres across, with a rounded top. Pour a second and a third spoon onto the same spot to see the heap grow.
flow.context: In this step you pour both liquids and compare the shapes they make.

flow.do: Ask your child to write what they thought, what they saw and why. Then link it to volcanoes together. Afterwards pour the batter and water into the bin or a compost pot, because the straws have been in mouths. Wash the tumblers and plates.
flow.say: Tell me what you guessed, what you saw and why you think it happened. Now think of magma with bubbles in it. What would runny magma do at the top of a volcano? What would sticky magma do?
flow.kid: Write what you thought, what you saw, and why. Then think: what would sticky magma do?
flow.think: If you shook a closed soda bottle and opened it, which volcano would it be like? What is the batter in that picture?
flow.parent: A good answer says the sticky liquid held the air longer and made a taller heap. Then give the link. Runny magma lets its bubbles go, so lava pours out and spreads into wide, low hills or floods, as in Hawaii and the Deccan. Sticky magma traps its bubbles until the push blows it apart into ash, and it piles into a steep cone, as at Krakatau. Then say what the test leaves out. Real magma is hotter than 700 degrees Celsius. Its bubbles are not blown in. They come out of the magma itself when the squeeze on it drops, the way fizz appears when a soda bottle is opened.
flow.context: In this step you say what the results show and connect them to two kinds of volcano.

activities.title: How thin is the ground? Draw the Earth to scale

materials.item: a sheet of plain paper, A4 size or larger
a ruler of 30 centimetres
a pencil with a fine point, and a red pen or crayon

activities.record: Keep the scale drawing. Write on it: 1 centimetre stands for 500 kilometres.
activities.context: In this activity you draw a wedge of the Earth with every layer at its true size. You guess how deep people have dug, and then you find out how thin the crust we live on really is.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a ruler laid from one corner, and pencil dots marked along it at three distances.
setup.caption: 1. From one corner, mark dots at 2.4, 7 and 12.7 centimetres along the ruler.

setup.art: The same sheet with the ruler turned to five different angles and three curved lines joining the dots into arcs.
setup.caption: 2. Turn the ruler and mark again, five times. Join the dots into three curves.

setup.art: A finished wedge of the Earth with inner core, outer core and mantle labelled, the outer edge drawn as one fine pencil line, and a child's red guess mark deep inside.
setup.caption: 3. The corner is the centre of the Earth. The outer curve is the ground.

flow.do: Before drawing, ask how far it is to the centre of the Earth, and how deep people have ever dug. Write both guesses on the back of the sheet.
flow.say: How far do you think it is from here to the centre of the Earth? And how deep is the deepest hole people have ever made? Tell me why you think so.
flow.kid: Guess how far it is to the centre of the Earth. Guess how deep people have dug. Write both guesses.
flow.parent: Accept any guess. Many children think people have dug most of the way down, or that mines reach the lava.
flow.context: This is the first step of the scale drawing. You guess before you measure.

flow.do: Lay the ruler from one corner of the sheet. Mark dots at 2.4, 7 and 12.7 centimetres. Turn the ruler a little, keeping zero on the corner, and mark again. Do this five times across the sheet. Join the dots into three smooth curves. Label the parts from the corner out: inner core, outer core, mantle.
flow.say: The corner is the centre of the Earth. One centimetre is 500 kilometres. The first curve is the edge of the solid inner core. The second is the edge of the liquid outer core. The last curve is the ground we stand on.
flow.kid: Mark dots at 2.4, 7 and 12.7 centimetres from the corner. Do it five times. Join the dots into curves.
flow.parent: The real sizes are 1,220 kilometres for the inner core, 3,480 kilometres to the top of the outer core, and 6,370 kilometres to the surface. Dividing each by 500 gives the centimetres. Let your child do one of the divisions.
flow.context: In this step you draw the inner core, the outer core and the mantle at their true sizes.

flow.do: Ask your child to mark in red how far in from the outer curve the deepest hole reaches. Then give the numbers. The crust under land is about 35 kilometres thick, which is less than 1 millimetre on the drawing. The deepest hole is 12 kilometres, which is a quarter of a millimetre.
flow.say: Mark where you think the deepest hole ends. Now here is the real number. The whole crust is thinner than your pencil line. The deepest hole does not even cross that line. What does that tell you about how we know the rest?
flow.kid: Mark your guess for the deepest hole in red. Then hear the real number. Look at your pencil line.

ask.q: If nobody has been below the crust, how could anyone know what is down there?
good: From earthquake waves that pass through.
By working it out from clues.

flow.think: Everything you have ever seen, every mountain and every sea, fits inside that pencil line. How does that feel?
flow.parent: 35 divided by 500 is 0.07 centimetres, or 0.7 millimetres. 12 divided by 500 is 0.024 centimetres. Mount Everest, at nearly 9 kilometres, would stand up by less than a fifth of a millimetre. Do not explain earthquake waves fully here. Leave the question open. The explanation cards answer it.
flow.context: In this step you find how thin the crust is, and how little of the Earth anyone has reached.

activities.title: Biscuit plates: three ways for plates to meet

materials.item: a flat steel plate
thick curd, hung curd or jam, spread 1 centimetre deep
plain flat biscuits, such as Marie or glucose biscuits
a small bowl of water

activities.record: Draw the three edges from the side, with arrows for which way the biscuits moved, and write the name of a real place under each.
activities.context: In this activity two biscuits stand for two plates, and a layer of curd stands for the soft, creeping rock below them. You make the plates move apart, push together and slide past, and you see what each edge does.

setup.art: A steel plate with a smooth layer of thick curd and two biscuits lying side by side on it, edges touching.
setup.caption: 1. Spread the curd. Lay two biscuits on it with their edges touching.

setup.art: Two hands pressing lightly on the biscuits and sliding them apart, with curd rising in the gap.
setup.caption: 2. Press lightly and slide them apart. Watch the gap.

setup.art: Two biscuits with wet, soft edges pushed together so the edges crumple up into a ridge.
setup.caption: 3. Wet one edge of each new biscuit. Push the wet edges together.

flow.do: Wash hands. Spread the curd on the plate. Lay two biscuits on it, edges touching. Press down lightly and slide them slowly apart by 2 centimetres. Look at what happens in the gap.
flow.say: These biscuits are two plates. The curd is the soft rock under them. Before you move them apart, guess what will happen in the gap. Now do it slowly.
flow.kid: Lay two biscuits on the curd. Press lightly. Slide them slowly apart. Watch the gap.

ask.q: What came up in the gap, and what would it be in the real Earth?

flow.parent: The curd wells up between the biscuits. In the Earth, hot mantle rock rises into the gap, part of it melts, and it cools into new sea floor. This is happening now at the Carlsberg Ridge under the Arabian Sea.
flow.context: This is the first step of Biscuit Plates. You make two plates move apart.

flow.do: Take two new biscuits. Dip one edge of each in water for 3 seconds. Lay them on the curd and push the wet edges slowly together. Then take a dry biscuit and push it against another dry one. Press its edge down a little so that it slides underneath.
flow.say: Now two plates push together. First with soft edges. What do the edges do? Now with a hard edge pressed down. Where does that plate go?
flow.kid: Wet one edge of two biscuits. Push the wet edges together. Then push a dry one under another.

ask.q: Which real place is like the crumpled wet edges?

flow.parent: The wet edges crumple and rise into a ridge. That is how the Himalaya formed, where two continents met and neither could dive. The dry biscuit sliding under is like sea floor diving into the mantle, as the Indian plate does under the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
flow.context: In this step you push two plates together in two ways: crumpling, and diving under.

flow.do: Take two dry biscuits. Hold them edge to edge, pressing the edges together firmly. Now try to slide one forward and the other back. Feel what your hands feel. Draw the three edges, then eat the dry biscuits.
flow.say: Press the edges together hard and slide them past each other. Does it slide smoothly? What do you feel just before it moves? What falls off?
flow.kid: Press two dry biscuits edge to edge. Slide one forward and one back. Feel what happens.

ask.q: What did you feel in your fingers just before the biscuits moved?
good: I had to push harder and harder.
Then they jerked and crumbs broke off.

flow.think: Which of the three edges would you least like to live beside? Which would you most like to visit?
flow.parent: The edges catch, the push builds, and then they jerk, with crumbs breaking off. That jerk is a small earthquake. Say that curd and biscuits show the shapes well, but they move in seconds. The real thing takes millions of years.
flow.context: In this step you slide two plates past each other and feel them stick and slip.

activities.title: Dots that make lines: map the world's volcanoes and earthquakes

materials.item: a world map you can draw on: a page from an old atlas, a photocopy, or an outline traced from a book or a phone screen
a school atlas or a phone map, to find the places
a red and a blue pencil or pen

activities.record: Keep the map. On the back, list the places that did not fit on a line, and one question you have about each.
activities.context: In this activity you mark 12 volcanoes and 12 large earthquakes on a world map. You find out for yourself that they are not scattered, and you find the few that break the pattern.

setup.art: A world outline map on a table with a red and a blue pencil and an open atlas beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Get a world map you can draw on, and an atlas to find places.

setup.art: The world map with red triangles and blue dots falling in a curve around the edge of the Pacific Ocean and in a line across the Himalaya.
setup.caption: 2. Mark volcanoes with red triangles and earthquakes with blue dots.

setup.art: The same map with a pencil line joining the marks into belts, and three marks circled that lie away from the belts.
setup.caption: 3. Join the marks that make lines. Circle the ones that do not fit.

flow.do: Lay out the map. Ask your child to draw five small crosses in pencil where earthquakes or volcanoes might be common, and to say why.
flow.say: Where in the world do you think volcanoes and earthquakes happen? Everywhere? In hot places? Near the sea? Put five crosses where you would expect them, and tell me your reason.
flow.kid: Put five pencil crosses where you think volcanoes and earthquakes happen. Say why.
flow.parent: Many children scatter the crosses evenly or put them in hot countries. Keep the crosses on the map to compare with later.
flow.context: This is the first step of the map. You guess where the dots will fall.

flow.do: Read out the 12 volcanoes one at a time. Your child finds each in the atlas and marks it with a red triangle.
flow.say: I will read a volcano and its country. Find it and mark it with a red triangle. After six, stop and look. Do you see any shape yet?
flow.kid: Find each volcano in the atlas. Mark it with a red triangle.
flow.parent: The 12 volcanoes: Barren Island (Andaman Sea, India). Krakatau (Indonesia). Merapi (Java, Indonesia). Pinatubo (Philippines). Fuji (Japan). Mount St Helens (north-west United States). Popocatepetl (Mexico). Cotopaxi (Ecuador). Etna (Sicily, Italy). Nyiragongo (eastern Congo). Hekla (Iceland). Kilauea (Hawaii). Help with the finding, but let your child place the mark.
flow.context: In this step you mark 12 volcanoes.

flow.do: Read out the 12 earthquakes. Your child marks each with a blue dot.
flow.say: Now the earthquakes. Mark each with a blue dot. Watch where the blue dots fall compared with the red triangles.
flow.kid: Mark each earthquake with a blue dot. Watch where they fall.
flow.parent: The 12 earthquakes: Bhuj, Gujarat, 2001. Sumatra, Indonesia, 2004. Kashmir, 2005. Nepal, 2015. Assam and Tibet, 1950. Latur, Maharashtra, 1993. Tohoku, Japan, 2011. Southern Chile, 1960. Alaska, 1964. San Francisco, 1906. Haiti, 2010. Southern Turkiye, 2023.
flow.context: In this step you mark 12 large earthquakes.

flow.do: Ask your child to join the marks that seem to lie on lines, and to circle any that sit alone. Compare with the five pencil crosses.
flow.say: What do you notice? Join the marks that make a line. Circle the ones that sit away from the lines. How close were your five crosses?
flow.kid: Join the marks that make lines. Circle the ones that sit alone.
flow.think: Why might so many people choose to live along these lines?
flow.parent: A ring appears around the Pacific, and a belt runs from Indonesia through the Himalaya to Italy. Kilauea sits alone in the Pacific. Bhuj and Latur sit away from the Himalayan line. Do not explain these yet. Ask your child what could cause a volcano or an earthquake away from an edge, and keep the question for the explanation cards.
flow.context: In this step you look for the pattern and for the places that break it.

activities.title: Ready at home: a shake drill and a look round the flat

materials.item: your own home
paper and a pencil

activities.record: Write a family plan on one page: the safe spot in each room, the things you decided to move, and where you will meet outside. Put it on the fridge or by the door.
activities.context: In this activity you practise what to do when the ground shakes, and you look round your home for things that could fall. Nobody can say when an earthquake will come, so being ready is the part that is in your hands.

setup.art: A child crouched under a sturdy wooden table, one arm over the back of the head and neck and one hand holding a table leg.
setup.caption: 1. Drop to your knees. Cover your head and neck. Hold on.

setup.art: A bedroom where a heavy suitcase sits on top of a tall cupboard beside a bed, with an arrow showing it being moved to the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Look for heavy things kept high up, above beds and seats.

setup.art: A family standing in an open space outside a block of flats, away from walls and wires.
setup.caption: 3. Choose an open place outside to meet afterwards.

flow.do: Sit together. Ask what your child would do if the floor began to shake right now. Listen to the whole answer before you say anything.
flow.say: Imagine the floor starts shaking now, hard enough that it is difficult to stand. What would you do in the first five seconds? Why that?
flow.kid: Imagine the floor starts shaking now. Say what you would do first. Say why.
flow.parent: Many children say they would run outside. In strong shaking people are hurt mostly by falling objects, breaking windows and stairs, so running is often the riskier choice. Hold that thought for the next step.
flow.context: This is the first step of the drill. You say what you would do before you learn the advice.

flow.do: In each room, choose the safest spot: under a sturdy table, or low beside an inside wall, away from windows and tall cupboards. Practise in each room. Drop to your knees and cover your head and neck with your arms. Hold on while a grown-up counts slowly to 20.
flow.say: India's disaster authority teaches three words: drop, cover, hold. Drop to your knees so you are not thrown down. Cover your head and neck. Hold on until the shaking stops. Let us find the best spot in this room.
flow.kid: Find the safest spot in each room. Drop to your knees. Cover your head and neck. Hold on for a count of 20.

ask.q: Why is under a strong table better than beside the window?
good: Things can fall on the table and not on me.

flow.parent: If there is no table, crouch beside a bed or an inside wall and cover the head and neck. In bed, stay there and cover the head with a pillow. Once the shaking stops, walk out by the stairs to open ground. Never use the lift. Be honest that experts discuss one case. In a weak building, a person on the ground floor who is a few steps from open ground may do better to get out at once.
flow.context: In this step you find a safe spot in every room and practise drop, cover, hold.

flow.do: Walk through the home together and only look. Find heavy things kept high: boxes on cupboards, pictures or shelves above beds, a television that could tip. A grown-up decides what to move lower and does the moving later.
flow.say: Now be a detective. If this room shook hard, what could fall? What is above your pillow? What is above the sofa? Show me, and I will decide what to move.
flow.kid: Walk through your home and look. Find heavy things kept high up. Show a grown-up.
flow.parent: The child only points. The lifting and any fixing of cupboards to walls is a grown-up's job for later. The most useful single change is to clear heavy things from above beds.
flow.context: In this step you look for things that could fall in strong shaking.

flow.do: Agree on an open place outside to meet after any earthquake. Then learn the beach rule together and say it aloud. Write the family plan.
flow.say: Here is the beach rule. If the ground shakes hard or for a long time, or if the sea pulls far back, leave the beach at once. Go to high ground or far inland, and tell others. Do not wait for anyone to announce it.
flow.kid: Choose where your family will meet outside. Learn the beach rule and say it aloud.

ask.q: The sea has pulled back and the wet sand is full of shells. What do you do?
good: Leave at once for high ground.
Go far from the sea and tell others.
I stay away from the bared sand.

flow.think: Being ready does not stop an earthquake. What does it change?
flow.parent: In 2004 many people walked out onto the bared sea bed to look. A girl of ten named Tilly Smith, on a beach in Thailand, remembered a school lesson, told her parents, and the beach was cleared in time. The first wave is often not the largest, so stay away for several hours.
flow.context: In this step you choose a meeting place and learn the sign of a tsunami.

projects.title: Seven days of a shaking planet: an earthquake diary

materials.item: a world map you can draw on, or the map from the Dots That Make Lines activity
a phone or computer with the internet, used with a grown-up, for 5 minutes a day
a notebook page ruled into a table
a pencil and a green pen

schedule.what: Rule the table and write your guess. Record today's largest earthquake in the world and today's largest in or near India.
Record the two earthquakes for the day and mark them on the map.
Record the two earthquakes for the day and mark them on the map.
Record the two earthquakes for the day and mark them on the map.
Record the two earthquakes for the day and mark them on the map.
Record the two earthquakes for the day and mark them on the map.
Record the last day. Look at the whole week and write what you found.

projects.record: A table of 7 days with the place, the magnitude and the depth of two earthquakes each day, a map with 14 green marks, and three sentences about what the week showed.
projects.context: In this project you keep a diary of real earthquakes for one week, using the public lists that seismologists publish. You find out how often the Earth shakes, where it shakes, and how many earthquakes nobody near you ever hears about.

setup.art: A notebook page ruled into columns headed day, place, magnitude and depth, with the first row filled in.
setup.caption: 1. Rule a table with a row for each day.

setup.art: A parent and child looking at a phone that shows a list of recent earthquakes with places and numbers.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, look up the list of recent earthquakes with a grown-up.

setup.art: A world map with a week of small green marks, most of them along the same belts as the earlier red and blue marks.
setup.caption: 3. Mark each one on your map in green.

flow.do: Rule a table with columns for the day, the place, the magnitude and the depth. Ask for a guess and write it down. Then open the list of recent earthquakes from India's National Centre for Seismology. The world map of the United States Geological Survey works too. Record the largest one in the world today and the largest one in or near India.
flow.say: How many earthquakes do you think will happen in the world this week that are big enough to be felt? Ten? A hundred? More? Write your guess. Now let us look at today's list.
flow.kid: Rule your table. Guess how many earthquakes will be felt this week. Then look up today's list with a grown-up.
flow.parent: Both lists are free and need no sign-in. The addresses are in the links for this lesson. If you have no internet, use the earthquake reports in a newspaper for the week and record what you find.
flow.context: This is the first day of the diary. You guess, and you record the first two earthquakes.

flow.do: On each of the next five days, spend 5 minutes. Record the day's largest earthquake in the world and the largest in or near India. Mark both on the map in green.
flow.say: Where was today's largest? How deep was it? Is it on one of the lines on your map, or away from them?
flow.kid: Each day, write down two earthquakes. Mark them on your map in green.
flow.wait: Come back to this once a day for five days.

ask.q: Did anyone you know feel today's earthquakes?
good: No, they were far away or small.
Most earthquakes are never felt by us.

flow.parent: On most days the world's largest will be between magnitude 5 and 6, and India's largest between 3 and 4.5. Many will be in the Himalaya, the Northeast or the Andaman Sea. If a day has none listed for India, write 'none' in the table. That is a result too.
flow.context: On these five days you add to the table and the map.

flow.do: On day 7, record the last pair. Then look at the whole week. Count how many of the 14 fall on the belts you found before. Find the deepest and the shallowest. Write three sentences about what the week showed.
flow.say: Look at your week. Where did most of them fall? Was your guess for the number too high or too low? What surprised you?
flow.kid: Count how many marks fall on the lines. Find the deepest earthquake. Write three sentences about your week.
flow.think: The Earth shook thousands of times this week and you felt none of it. What does that say about how much you can know from your own senses?
flow.parent: Around the world, about 100,000 earthquakes a year are strong enough to be felt, which is roughly 2,000 a week. About 15 a year reach magnitude 7. Your child recorded only 14 of one week's thousands. Ask what the diary leaves out, since it holds only the largest of each day.
flow.context: On the last day you look for patterns in a week of real earthquakes.

challenges.title: The Lemon Tower: build something that stands when the ground moves
challenges.problem: Build a tower from newspaper and tape that holds a lemon at least 30 centimetres above a tray. Then shake the tray. The tower passes if the lemon is still up after 10 seconds of strong shaking. There are many good answers, and builders in different parts of India found different ones.
constraints: Use only 10 sheets of newspaper and 1 metre of tape.
The lemon must sit at least 30 centimetres above the tray.
The tower stands on a tray, a large steel plate or a chopping board that someone can slide.
You may tape the tower's feet to the tray with 4 small pieces from your 1 metre.
materials: a lemon, or a small potato or ball of the same size
a tray, a large steel plate or a chopping board
a small book and 6 round pencils, for the last step
general: A wide base and a narrow top. A tower that is wider at the bottom is harder to tip.
Triangles. A square frame leans over into a diamond when it is pushed. A slanting strip across it makes two triangles, which hold their shape.
A light top. Keep the weight low. The more weight is high up, the harder the shaking throws it about.
creative: Let the ground move without the building. A tower standing on round pencils stays nearly in place while the tray slides under it. Engineers call this base isolation. The hospital at Bhuj was rebuilt in this way after 2001.
Go round. The bhunga houses of Kutch are round, with a light roof. Builders there chose the shape after an earthquake in 1819, and many bhungas stood in 2001 when newer buildings fell.
Bend, do not break. In the timber-laced walls of Kashmir and the bamboo and reed houses of Assam, light wooden frames flex and soak up the shaking. A rigid wall cracks.
challenges.your_turn: Now change the rules yourself. Make the tower twice as tall, or carry two lemons, or use only 5 sheets. Or invent a way nobody has listed here. Draw your design first and say why you think it will work.
challenges.context: This is a building challenge. Earthquakes cannot be stopped or foretold, so the question engineers ask is how to build things that stay up. You try several answers with newspaper, tape and a lemon.

setup.art: A sheet of newspaper being rolled from one corner into a long thin tube, with a piece of tape holding it closed.
setup.caption: 1. Roll sheets of newspaper into tight tubes and tape them.

setup.art: A tower about 30 centimetres tall made of newspaper tubes with slanting cross-pieces, a lemon resting in a paper cup shape at the top, standing on a steel tray.
setup.caption: 2. Build a tower at least 30 centimetres tall with a seat for the lemon.

setup.art: Two hands sliding the tray quickly from side to side on a table while a child watches the lemon and counts.
setup.caption: 3. Slide the tray from side to side for 10 seconds. Does the lemon stay up?

flow.do: Read the problem and the four rules together. Give your child paper and a pencil. Ask for a sketch of the tower before any newspaper is touched, with one sentence on why it will stand.
flow.say: You have 10 sheets, 1 metre of tape and a lemon. The lemon must stay 30 centimetres up while I shake the tray. Draw your idea first. What will stop it from tipping?
flow.kid: Read the rules. Draw your tower before you build. Say why it will stand.

ask.q: What do you think will fail first when the tray shakes?

flow.parent: Do not suggest a design. A plain tube standing on end is a fine first try, and its failure will teach more than your advice.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Lemon Tower. You plan before you build.

flow.do: Roll sheets of newspaper from one corner into tight tubes and tape each one closed. Join the tubes into a tower. Make a seat at the top for the lemon. Measure that the seat is at least 30 centimetres above the tray.
flow.say: Roll the tubes tight, because a tight tube is much stiffer than a loose one. Build your design. Tell me if you change your mind about something as you go.
flow.kid: Roll the newspaper into tight tubes. Tape them. Build your tower. Check that it is 30 centimetres tall.
flow.parent: Tear the tape by hand, or have pieces ready in advance. A sheet rolled from the corner makes a tube about 70 centimetres long that can be folded or torn into shorter pieces. If the tape is running out, suggest slotting one tube inside another.
flow.context: In this step you build the tower from tubes of newspaper.

flow.do: Put the lemon on the tower. A grown-up slides the tray from side to side for 10 seconds at each of three levels. Gentle is 2 centimetres each way. Medium is 5 centimetres. Strong is 10 centimetres, twice a second. Write what happened at each level.
flow.say: Gentle first. Count to ten with me. Now medium. Now strong. Watch closely and tell me where it bent, and what moved first.
flow.kid: Put the lemon on top. Watch the tower as the tray shakes. Say where it bends first.

ask.q: Where did the tower bend or break first?
good: At the bottom of the legs.
It leaned into a diamond shape.

flow.parent: Keep the shaking the same for every tower, so that the test is fair. Most first towers pass gentle and fail at medium, usually by leaning over at the joints or tipping from the base.
flow.context: In this step you test the tower at three strengths of shaking.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the surprising ones together. Choose one change and make it. Test again at the level that failed. Then try one more thing. Untape the feet and stand the tower on a small book resting on 6 round pencils. Shake the tray gently along the direction the pencils roll.
flow.say: Builders have found many answers. Some make the building stiffer. Some let it bend. Some let the ground move without it. Which one do you want to try? What happened to the lemon on the pencils?
flow.kid: Choose one change and make it. Test again. Then stand the tower on round pencils and shake.
flow.think: A stiff tower and a bendy tower can both pass. Which would you rather be inside, and why?
flow.parent: On the pencils the book and tower stay nearly still while the tray slides beneath, as long as the shaking is along the rolling direction. Say honestly that no building is earthquake-proof. Engineers aim for a building that may be damaged but does not fall, so that the people inside can walk out.
flow.context: In this step you improve the tower and try the idea of letting the ground move under it.

items.p: Which layer of the Earth do we live on?
items.why: We live on the crust, the thin outer layer. The mantle begins tens of kilometres below us, and nobody has ever reached it.

items.p: The layer of liquid metal deep inside the Earth is the outer ____.
items.why: The outer core is liquid iron and nickel. The inner core, at the very centre, is solid.

items.p: The mantle is a sea of melted rock.
items.why: False. The mantle is solid rock that creeps very slowly. We know because S waves pass through it, and S waves do not pass through liquids.

items.p: Draw a slice of the Earth from the surface to the centre. Label the crust, mantle, outer core and inner core.
items.a: Four layers in the right order, with the crust drawn as the thinnest and the mantle as the thickest.
items.why: The order from outside in is crust, mantle, outer core, inner core. A strong drawing makes the crust a thin line, because it is less than one hundredth of the way down.

items.p: What is a plate?
opts: A huge moving slab of crust and upper mantle
A layer of lava under the ground
items.why: A plate is a slab of the crust and the stiff top of the mantle. If you chose lava, remember that the rock under the plates is solid and only creeps.

items.p: Match each plate movement to what it makes.
pairs: New sea floor forms in the gap
A sea-floor plate pushes against another plate
One plate dives and volcanoes grow above
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each kind of edge leaves its own mark. Gaps fill with new rock, diving plates feed volcanoes, continents crumple, and sliding edges stick and slip.

items.p: Put these in order to tell how an earthquake happens.
a: The rock at the fault stays stuck
The rock bends and stores energy
items.why: The plates never stop, but friction holds the fault. The rock bends like a stretched rubber band until the stuck patch gives way, and the stored energy travels out as waves.

items.p: What do we call the place on the surface straight above the start of an earthquake?
items.why: The epicentre is on the surface. The focus is the place underground where the slip begins. A crater belongs to a volcano.

items.p: Melted rock that is still under the ground is called ____.
items.why: It is magma while it is underground and lava once it comes out onto the surface.

items.p: Lava is magma that has reached the surface.
items.why: True. It is the same melted rock. Only the name changes when it comes out.

items.p: Sort each word by where it belongs.
items.a: as given
items.why: Faults, epicentres and seismic waves describe an earthquake. Magma, vents, ash and craters describe a volcano. Plate edges are where most of both are found.

items.p: Why does the edge of the Pacific Ocean have so many volcanoes and earthquakes?
opts: Many plate edges run along it
The water there is the deepest
items.why: Sea-floor plates dive under other plates all round the Pacific. Depth and warmth of the water do not make earthquakes. The moving rock does.

items.p: The ground feels still. Give two pieces of evidence that it is moving.
items.a: Any two of these: satellite markers move a few centimetres a year. Sea shells are found on Himalayan peaks. Earthquakes show sudden slips. The sea floor is youngest at the ridges. Matching fossils lie on lands now far apart.
items.why: A strong answer gives evidence someone measured or found, and does not only say that a book says so.

items.p: In your own words, why can nobody tell the day of the next earthquake?
items.a: A good answer says the stuck rock is deep and cannot be seen, that nobody can measure how close it is to slipping, and that tiny differences decide when it goes. It may use the Sticking Box as an example.
items.why: We know where the squeeze is building, but not the breaking point of the rock. In the Sticking Box test the waits were never exactly the same, even though you could see the band.

items.p: Two farmers live on the slope of a volcano that last erupted 90 years ago.

views.says: The soil here is the best for a hundred kilometres. My family has eaten well for three generations. I am staying.
A volcano that has erupted once will erupt again. No harvest is worth my children's lives. I am moving to the plain.

items.ask: Which farmer do you agree with more? What would you want to find out before you decided?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and names something to find out, such as how often the volcano erupts, if it is being watched, and how fast people could leave.
items.why: Both are right about a fact. Volcanic soil is rich, and a quiet volcano can wake. Millions of people around the world make this choice, and many stay and keep a plan to leave quickly.

items.p: A plate moves 4 centimetres every year. How many centimetres does it move in 25 years?
items.why: 4 times 25 is 100 centimetres, which is 1 metre. In one long human life a plate moves about as far as a child is tall.

items.p: Put India's journey in order, from the oldest event to the newest.
a: The Deccan lava floods pour out
items.why: India left Gondwana, lost Madagascar about 88 million years ago, crossed a hot spot about 66 million years ago and met Asia about 50 million years ago. The Himalaya have been rising since.

items.p: What are the Deccan Traps mostly made of?
items.why: They are layer upon layer of basalt from lava floods. Sandstone and coral rock form in water, in a quite different way.

items.p: Barren Island in the Andaman Sea is an active volcano.
items.why: True. It erupted in 1991 after well over a century of quiet, and it has erupted on and off ever since.

items.p: The tsunami of 2004 began with a giant earthquake under the sea near the island of ____.
items.why: The fault off Sumatra, in Indonesia, slipped along about 1,300 kilometres, as far north as the Andaman Islands.

items.p: What makes most tsunamis?
opts: A sudden jump of the sea floor
items.why: A tsunami starts when the sea floor lifts or drops and moves all the water above it. Wind makes ordinary waves. The Moon's pull makes tides, which are a different thing.

items.p: Match each place to what you would find there.
pairs: A large earthquake far inside a plate
Hills cut into steps of basalt
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each place holds one piece of India's story: old cracks that still slip, lava from the split with Madagascar, a diving plate, the Deccan floods and the lost Tethys Sea.

items.p: A tsunami crosses deep ocean at 700 kilometres an hour. A coast is 1,400 kilometres away. How many hours until it arrives?
items.why: 1,400 divided by 700 is 2 hours. That is enough time to clear a coast, if a warning is sent and people know what to do.

items.p: How much more does the ground move in a magnitude 7 earthquake than in a magnitude 6?
items.why: Each whole step in magnitude means ten times more ground movement. If you chose 'a little more', remember that the scale multiplies and does not add.

items.p: An earthquake has one magnitude, but the shaking it causes differs from place to place.
items.why: True. Magnitude measures the size at the source. How hard the ground shakes at your home depends on your distance and on the soil under you.

items.p: Sort each clue: does it belong to runny lava or to sticky magma?
items: spreads in floods, as in the Deccan
traps its bubbles until it bursts
items.a: as given
items.why: Runny lava lets its bubbles go and flows far. Sticky magma holds its bubbles until the push blows it apart, and what falls builds a steep cone.

items.p: Bhuj is far from any plate edge. Explain how it could still have a great earthquake.
items.a: A good answer says that India is squeezed as it pushes into Asia, that old cracks from the time India broke from other lands lie under Kutch, and that one of them slipped under the squeeze.
items.why: The push at the edge is felt far inside the plate. Old faults are weak places, and they can store the squeeze for a very long time before they slip.

items.p: Draw India meeting Asia from the side. Show the Himalaya. Star one place where rock sticks and slips.
items.a: A slab from the left sliding under or against a slab on the right, with crumpled mountains above the join and a star on the sloping surface between the two.
items.why: The Indian plate pushes under the edge of Asia along a sloping fault. The rock above crumples into the Himalaya, and the great earthquakes start on that sloping surface.

items.p: About 66 million years ago the giant dinosaurs died out. Scientists do not fully agree why.

views.who: Luis and Walter Alvarez, in 1980, and most scientists today
views.says: An asteroid about 10 kilometres wide struck where Mexico is now. Its dust lies in a thin layer of rock all round the world.
The Deccan eruptions in India had already filled the air with gases and harmed life in the seas. The lava did most of the damage.
Both mattered. Life was already under strain from the lava when the asteroid struck.

items.ask: Which view seems strongest to you? What evidence would you want to see to be more sure?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a view, gives one piece of evidence for it, and names a test, such as dating the lava layers more exactly or finding fossils from just before the asteroid.
items.why: This is a live debate. The asteroid has the most support, but the lava's part is still being measured. No answer here is marked wrong if it gives evidence.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Bhuj, Latur, Koyna, Kathmandu.
items.a: Kathmandu, because it lies along a plate edge, in the Himalaya. The earthquakes at Bhuj, Latur and Koyna happened far inside the Indian plate.
items.why: Three of these places surprised people because they are far from the edge. Any other answer with a true reason also counts.

items.p: A friend says South India is safe from earthquakes. What would you tell her? Give an example.
items.a: A good answer says the danger is lower but not zero, and gives an example: Latur in 1993, Koyna in 1967, Coimbatore in 1900, or the tsunami of 2004 that reached Tamil Nadu and Kerala from far away.
items.why: Rare is not the same as never. Earthquakes inside a plate come seldom, so people are less prepared for them.

items.p: The name Gondwana comes from the land of the ____ people of central India.
items.why: Geologists named the old southern land after the region of the Gond people, where the first rocks of that age were studied.

items.p: Why does a P wave reach a seismograph before an S wave from the same earthquake?
items.why: Both leave at the same moment. P waves travel at about 6 kilometres a second in the crust and S waves at about 4, so the P wave wins the race.

items.p: A P wave travels 6 kilometres a second. A seismograph is 300 kilometres away. After how many seconds does it arrive?
items.why: 300 divided by 6 is 50 seconds. Seismologists use arrival times like this from many stations to find where an earthquake began.

items.p: After a great earthquake, S waves never arrive on the far side of the Earth. What does this tell us, and why?
items.a: A good answer says there is a liquid layer deep inside, the outer core, because S waves shake rock from side to side and a liquid does not spring back sideways.
items.why: The missing S waves are a shadow cast by the liquid outer core. This is how people learned about a layer nobody has seen.

items.p: People have drilled through the crust and into the mantle.
items.why: False. The deepest hole is about 12 kilometres deep, and the crust under land is about 35 kilometres thick. Everything known about the mantle comes from waves and from rock that volcanoes bring up.

items.p: Where is the rock of the sea floor youngest?
opts: It is the same age everywhere
items.why: New sea floor forms at the ridges and moves away on both sides, so it gets older with distance. This was strong evidence that plates move.

items.p: Fossils of one plant, Glossopteris, lie in India, Africa, Australia and Antarctica. Give two possible explanations. Which fits better?
items.a: One: the lands were once joined and later moved apart. Two: the seeds crossed the oceans, or land bridges once joined the continents and later sank. A good answer says which fits better and why, for example that the rocks and many other fossils match too.
items.why: Both ideas were held by real scientists. The joined-lands idea won because the sea floor shows no sunken bridges, and because the plates can now be measured moving.

items.p: Match each person to what they found.
pairs: The Earth has a solid inner core
A rift valley runs along the ocean ridge
An instrument that sensed distant earthquakes, in 132 CE
Earthquake waves show the Earth has a core
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These five worked in Denmark, Germany, the United States, China and India. Oldham did his work on earthquake waves at the Geological Survey of India, after the Assam earthquake of 1897.

items.p: A place where volcanoes form far from any plate edge, above unusually hot rock, is called a hot ____.
items.why: Hawaii and Réunion sit on hot spots. What feeds them is still argued.

items.p: The volcanoes of Hawaii sit on the edge of a plate.
items.why: False. Hawaii is in the middle of the Pacific plate, thousands of kilometres from any edge. It is one of the places that breaks the rule.

items.p: Can other animals sense an earthquake before it comes?

views.who: Martin Wikelski and his team, in 2020
views.says: Our tagged cows, sheep and dogs moved about more in the hours before nearby earthquakes. Together they gave a signal.

views.who: Heiko Woith and other seismologists, in 2018
views.says: We read 180 studies. Most were stories told afterwards, with no record of ordinary days to compare with. The evidence is too weak so far.

items.ask: Which view do you find stronger? What test would change your mind?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a view and describes a test, such as tagging animals in many places for years and counting how often they were restless with no earthquake.
items.why: Both sides are careful scientists. One has found a pattern on one farm. The other asks for the same pattern in many places before believing it. Neither has been shown wrong.

items.p: Put the steps of a tsunami warning in order.
a: The sea floor jumps in an earthquake
Seismographs record the waves within minutes
A sensor on the sea floor feels the wave pass
The warning centre sends an alert
People on the coast move to high ground
items.why: Seismic waves travel much faster than the tsunami, so the earthquake is found first. The sea-floor sensor then confirms that a wave was really made, and the alert goes out.

items.p: How does an earthquake alert on a phone work?
opts: Sensors catch the first fast waves and send word ahead
It predicts the earthquake a day before
items.why: The earthquake has already begun. Sensors near it catch the P waves, and a radio message outruns the slower, stronger waves by a few seconds. It is a warning and not a prediction.

items.p: Draw what lies under Barren Island. Label the diving plate, where rock melts, and the magma's path.
items.a: A sloping slab going down under the island, a patch of melting above the slab at depth, and a pipe or chain of blobs rising from it to the volcano.
items.why: The Indian plate dives under the Burma plate there. Water from the diving slab helps the rock above it to melt, and the magma rises to feed the volcano. A drawing with these three parts is a good model, even if the shapes differ.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Deccan Traps, Barren Island, St Mary's Islands, the Himalaya.
items.a: The Himalaya, because they are sea-floor rock that was folded and lifted. The other three are made of lava.
items.why: Three were built by volcanoes and one by a collision. Any other answer with a true reason also counts.

items.p: Design a fair test of this claim: dogs bark more before earthquakes. What would you record, and for how long?
items.a: A good answer records barking every day for a long time, on ordinary days as well as before earthquakes, in many homes, and has the records written down before anyone knows an earthquake came.
items.why: A memory after the event is not evidence, because people remember the barking that fits. A fair test counts the ordinary days too.

items.p: Sort each statement: is it settled, or still argued by scientists?
items: Plates move a few centimetres a year
Hot spots are fed by plumes from the deep mantle
Deccan lava helped to end the giant dinosaurs
India was once joined to Antarctica
Farm animals sense earthquakes hours ahead
items.a: as given
items.why: Settled does not mean it can never change. It means the evidence is strong and has been checked many ways. The argued ones still need better evidence.

quiz.p: How do we know what the inside of the Earth is like?
opts: From how earthquake waves travel through it
From holes drilled to the centre
quiz.why: Earthquake waves bend, slow down or stop as they pass through different layers. The deepest hole is only 12 kilometres deep, out of 6,370.

quiz.p: Which layer of the Earth is the thickest?
quiz.why: The mantle is about 2,900 kilometres thick. The crust is the thinnest layer, and the inner core is a ball about 1,220 kilometres in radius.

quiz.p: About how fast do plates move?
opts: As fast as a person walks
quiz.why: Plates move 2 to 10 centimetres a year. If you chose 'they stay', remember that satellites measure the movement every day.

quiz.p: What happens where two plates carrying continents push together?
quiz.why: Continent rock is too light to dive, so it crumples and piles up, as in the Himalaya. A new ocean opens where plates move apart.

quiz.p: What makes the ground shake in an earthquake?
quiz.why: Rock bends while a fault is stuck and then slips. The wind idea is very old and was given up when faults were studied.

quiz.p: The focus of an earthquake is underground, and the epicentre is on the surface above it.
quiz.why: True. The slip begins at the focus. The epicentre is the point on the map straight above.

opts: Their lava is colder than ice
quiz.why: Thick magma holds its bubbles until the push blows it apart. Runny magma lets the gas out, and its lava flows quietly.

quiz.p: A volcano has been quiet for 300 years. What is the most truthful thing to say?
quiz.why: A volcano's life is far longer than 300 years. Barren Island was quiet for well over a century before 1991.

quiz.p: Where do most earthquakes and volcanoes happen?
quiz.why: Marked on a map, they fall into narrow belts along plate edges. Iceland and Alaska are cold and have plenty of both.

quiz.p: Which of these lies far from any plate edge?
quiz.why: Latur is deep inside the Indian plate, which is why its earthquake in 1993 surprised people. The other two lie along plate edges.
The sea floor between India and Asia was squeezed and lifted. That is why the high rocks hold sea shells and no lava.

opts: Barren Island, in the Andaman Sea
quiz.why: Barren Island sits above a diving plate. Mahabaleshwar is old Deccan lava that stopped flowing about 66 million years ago.

quiz.p: Which of these can scientists do today?
opts: Warn seconds after an earthquake starts
Name the day a week ahead

applications: Tsunami warning: the centre at INCOIS in Hyderabad watches seismographs and sea-floor sensors day and night, and sends alerts to every coastal state.
Building rules: India's earthquake map tells engineers how strong a school, a hospital or a bridge must be in each district.
Phone alerts: phones and sensors in parts of India can now warn people a few seconds before strong shaking arrives.
Heat from the ground: in volcanic places such as Iceland and Indonesia, hot rock underground makes steam that drives power stations. India is testing this at Puga in Ladakh.
Farming: the black soil made from Deccan basalt grows much of India's cotton, jowar and tur dal.
Stone to build with: basalt was carved into the caves of Ajanta, Ellora and Elephanta, and granite into the temples of Thanjavur and Mamallapuram.
Finding metals: copper, gold and many other metals collect where magma once rose, so geologists use the plate map to decide where to search.

open_questions.q: Why does one small slip on a fault stop, while another grows into a giant earthquake?
open_questions.why_open: Both start in the same way. Nobody can see the stuck patches kilometres underground, and tiny differences in the rock seem to decide the outcome.

open_questions.q: When did plates first begin to move, and why does only the Earth have them?
open_questions.why_open: Venus is nearly the same size and has no moving plates. Estimates for the Earth's first plates range from 4,000 million to under 1,000 million years ago, because so little rock from that time is left.

open_questions.q: What feeds the hot spots, such as the one that made the Deccan Traps?
open_questions.why_open: Earthquake waves give only a blurred picture of the deep mantle, and the pictures can be read as deep plumes or as shallow melting.

open_questions.q: How much did the Deccan eruptions add to the death of the giant dinosaurs?
open_questions.why_open: The lava and the asteroid came within a few hundred thousand years of each other, and rock dating is not yet fine enough to pull their effects apart.

open_questions.q: Do other animals sense something before an earthquake, and if so, what?
open_questions.why_open: Large earthquakes are rare and cannot be arranged, so it takes many years of tagging animals in many places to get enough fair records.

open_questions.q: When will the next great Himalayan earthquake come?
open_questions.why_open: Measurements show the squeeze is building, but nobody can measure how close the deep rock is to its breaking point.

maths.problem: The Indian plate moves about 5 centimetres every year. A girl is 9 years old. How far has the ground under her home travelled since she was born?
maths.explain: 5 times 9 is 45. That is about the length of her arm.
maths.context: Satellites measure the Indian plate moving north-east, a little every year.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a small yearly movement by a number of years shows how a movement too slow to see adds up.

maths.problem: At 5 centimetres a year, how many years does the Indian plate take to move 1 kilometre? One kilometre is 100,000 centimetres.
maths.explain: 100,000 divided by 5 is 20,000. The first farming villages are only about 10,000 years old.
maths.context: Plates move slowly, but they have a very long time to do it.
maths.why_maths: Changing kilometres to centimetres lets you compare a plate's journey with a speed measured in centimetres.

maths.problem: In your scale drawing, 1 centimetre stands for 500 kilometres. The mantle is about 2,900 kilometres thick. How many centimetres thick is it on the drawing?
maths.explain: 2,900 divided by 500 is 5.8. On the same drawing the crust is less than 1 millimetre.
maths.context: In the scale drawing of the Earth, every real distance is divided by the same number.
maths.why_maths: A scale lets a thing far too big to see fit on a page with all its parts in the right proportion.

maths.problem: Each step of 1 in magnitude means the ground moves 10 times more. How many times more does the ground move in a magnitude 8 earthquake than in a magnitude 5?
maths.explain: From 5 to 8 is three steps. 10 times 10 times 10 is 1,000.
maths.context: Magnitude is a scale that multiplies. It does not add.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying by ten again and again explains why a magnitude 8 is a different kind of event from a magnitude 5.

maths.problem: P waves travel about 6 kilometres every second and S waves about 4. A town is 120 kilometres from an earthquake. How many seconds pass between the P wave and the S wave?
maths.explain: 120 divided by 6 is 20 seconds for the P wave. 120 divided by 4 is 30 seconds for the S wave. 30 take away 20 is 10.
maths.context: The gap between the two waves is what an early warning system uses.
maths.why_maths: Dividing distance by speed gives the travel time, and the difference between two travel times is the warning a town can get.

maths.problem: In the Sticking Box test, the waits before four jumps were 9, 12, 7 and 12 counts. What was the average wait? Was any wait exactly the average?
maths.explain: 9 and 12 and 7 and 12 make 40. 40 divided by 4 is 10. None of the four waits was 10.
maths.context: In the Sticking Box test you counted how long the box waited before each jump.
maths.why_maths: An average tells you roughly how often something happens. It does not tell you when the next one will come, and that is the limit of earthquake forecasting.

maths.problem: The deepest hole ever drilled is 12 kilometres deep. The centre of the Earth is about 6,400 kilometres down. About what fraction of the way did the drill go?
maths.explain: 6,400 divided by 12 is about 533, so the hole is about one five-hundredth of the way.
maths.context: Nobody has reached below the crust, so almost all we know about the inside comes from waves.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how small the part we have touched is, compared with the whole.

maths.problem: The Deccan lava covers about 500,000 square kilometres. India's land is about 3,300,000 square kilometres. Is the lava nearer to one tenth, one sixth or one third of India?
maths.explain: One tenth of 3,300,000 is 330,000. One sixth is 550,000. One third is 1,100,000. 500,000 is closest to 550,000.
maths.context: The Deccan Traps are one of the largest lava fields on Earth.
maths.why_maths: Estimating with round fractions turns a huge number into something you can picture on a map.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, geologists were sure that the continents had always stood where they are. To explain why the same fossils lay on both sides of an ocean, they imagined land bridges that had later sunk. It was a fair idea, because nobody had ever felt a continent move. In 1912 Alfred Wegener, a German weather scientist, said the continents had once been joined and had drifted apart. He was laughed at, because he could not name a force strong enough. He died in Greenland in 1930. In 1952 Marie Tharp, an American map-maker, was plotting depth readings from ships. Women were not allowed on the ships, so she worked from the numbers. She found a deep valley running down the middle of the ridge under the Atlantic, as if the sea floor were pulling apart there. Her own colleague first brushed it off as 'girl talk'. Then earthquakes were plotted on her map, and they fell along the same valley. In 1963 striped magnetic patterns in the sea floor showed that new rock is made at the ridges. By the late 1960s, most geologists had changed their minds.
how_we_found_out.who: Alfred Wegener, Marie Tharp, and Frederick Vine, Drummond Matthews and Lawrence Morley, who explained the magnetic stripes
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Geologists held that the continents never move, and that sunken land bridges explained matching fossils. Marie Tharp's map of a rift in the ocean ridge, the earthquakes along it and the magnetic stripes beside it showed that the sea floor spreads and the continents travel.
how_we_found_out.context: Do continents stay where they are? This card tells how an idea that was laughed at for fifty years turned out to be right, and who found the evidence.
